text: Two days after Barack Obama was sworn in as president of the United States, the Pew Research Center released a poll ranking the issues that Americans said were the most important priorities for this year. At the top of the list were several concerns — jobs and the economy — related to the current recession. Farther down, well after terrorism, deficit reduction and energy (and even something the pollsters characterized as “moral decline”) was climate change. It was priority No. 20. That was last place.</br></br>AN ANTHROPOLOGIST OBSERVED HOW THE BEHAVIOR OF POOR UGANDAN FARMERS COULD BE INFLUENCED BY WHETHER THEY LISTENED TO CRUCIAL RAINY-SEASON RADIO BROADCASTS IN GROUPS OR AS INDIVIDUALS. FARMERS IN‘COMMUNITY GROUPS’ ACHIEVED CONSENSUS AND MADE BETTER USE OF THE FORECAST.</br></br>at Columbia University, where a few dozen academics had assembled for a two-day conference on the environment. In many respects, the Pew rankings were a suitable backdrop for the get-together, a meeting of researchers affiliated with something called CRED, or the Center for Research on Environmental Decisions. A branch of behavioral research situated at the intersection of psychology and economics, decision science focuses on the mental processes that shape our choices, behaviors and attitudes. The field’s origins grew mostly out of the work, beginning in the 1970s, of Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, two psychologists whose experiments have demonstrated that people can behave unexpectedly when confronted with simple choices. We have many automatic biases — we’re more averse to losses than we are interested in gains, for instance — and we make repeated errors in judgment based on our tendency to use shorthand rules to solve problems. We can also be extremely susceptible to how questions are posed. Would you undergo surgery if it had a 20 percent mortality rate? What if it had an 80 percent survival rate? It’s the same procedure, of course, but in various experiments, responses from patients can differ markedly.</br></br>Over the past few decades a great deal of research has addressed how we make decisions in financial settings or when confronted with choices having to do with health care and consumer products. A few years ago, a Columbia psychology professor named David H. Krantz teamed up with Elke Weber — who holds a chair at Columbia’s business school as well as an appointment in the school’s psychology department — to assemble an interdisciplinary group of economists, psychologists and anthropolo- gists from around the world who would examine decision-making related to environmental issues. Aided by a $6 million grant from the National Science Foundation, CRED has the primary objective of studying how perceptions of risk and uncertainty shape our responses to climate change and other weather phenomena like hurricanes and droughts. The goal, in other words, isn’t so much to explore theories about how people relate to nature, which has been a longtime pursuit of some environmental psychologists and even academics like the Harvard biologist E.O. Wilson. Rather, it is to finance laboratory and field experiments in North America, South America, Europe and Africa and then place the findings within an environmental context.</br></br>It isn’t immediately obvious why such studies are necessary or even valuable. Indeed, in the United States scientific community, where nearly all dollars for climate investigation are directed toward physical or biological projects, the notion that vital environmental solutions will be attained through social-science research — instead of improved climate models or innovative technologies — is an aggressively insurgent view. You might ask the decision scientists, as I eventually did, if they aren’t overcomplicating matters. Doesn’t a low-carbon world really just mean phasing out coal and other fossil fuels in favor of clean-energy technologies, domestic regulations and international treaties? None of them disagreed. Some smiled patiently. But all of them wondered if I had underestimated the countless group and individual decisions that must precede any widespread support for such technologies or policies. “Let’s start with the fact that climate change is anthropogenic,” Weber told me one morning in her Columbia office. “More or less, people have agreed on that. That means it’s caused by human behavior. That’s not to say that engineering solutions aren’t important. But if it’s caused by human behavior, then the solution probably also lies in changing human behavior.”

text: THE human side of the recession, in the new media genre that’s been called “recession porn,” is the story of an incremental descent from excess to frugality, from ease to austerity. This demographic, the working poor, have already been living in an economic depression of their own. From their point of view "the economy," as a shared condition, is a fiction.</br></br>This spring, f tracked down a couple of the people I had met while working on my 2001 book, “Nickel and Dimed," in which I worked in low-wage jobs like wait-ressing and housecleaning, and I found them no more gripped by the recession than by “American Idol”; things were pretty much “same old.” The woman I called Melissa in the book was still working at Wal-Mart, though in nine years, her wages had risen to $10 an hour from $7. “Caroline,” who is increasingly disabled by diabetes and heart disease, now lives with a grown son and subsists on occasional cleaning and catering jobs. We phatted about grandchildren and church, without any mention of exceptional hardship.</br></br>As with Denise Smith, whom I recently met through • tile. It may look like just a marina and a campground, but with construction nearly completed, the Lake Okeechobee Outpost has become a test of whether the exuberance of coastal Florida can find a home in the state’s agricultural heart.</br></br>Hal Stankard is the outpost’s general manager. In a town of muddy pickups, he drives a Toyota Prius, wears golf shirts the color of citrus and sees the marina as a stopover for the hundreds of boaters who use the lake to cross from one Florida coast to the other.</br></br>"This is going to be the introduction of economic help for the whole area," Mr. Stankard said recently, staring at the marina from an empty building that will be a Tiki bar and upscale restaurant in a few months. “Think about what it will be like if we can fill this place with 80,90 boats, yachts even.”

text: Baby boomers have lived during an era of unparalleled prosperity. So when this deep recession hit — at a time when boomers were advancing to middle-and late-middle age — much was written about them being too spoiled to cope.</br></br>Not so. A look at recent employment data indicates that boomers have persevered in • these hard times, and are less likely to grow discouraged and quit the job hunt than younger workers are.</br></br>“Older adults are not giving up," said Steven Hippie, a Bureau of Labor Statistics economist. Despite the fact that the unemployment rate for baby boomers has doubled since the start of the recession, what the federal government calls their “labor participation rate" — the number of 45- to 64-year-olds working or actively seeking work — has remained unchanged. In contrast, every other age group has shown a decline.</br></br>“Older workers don’t have the choice of withdrawing from the labor force,” said Mr. Hippie, pointing out that they have mortgages to pay, health issues and retirement to worry about, as well as children to put through college.</br></br>Tory Johnson, owner of Women for Hire, which for the last decade has run job fairs in America’s 10 largest cities, has been struck by the toughness of the boomer work force. "With the 20- and 30-somethings, the attitude is, ‘No one is hiring, what’s the point of going to a job fair?”' Ms. Johnson said. “With the boomers, it’s, ‘Even if there's one job, I'll try.’” At her 16 job fairs so far in 2009, she said, attendance is up 10 percent over all, and it's because of boomers; every other age group has declined.

text: Growing dissatisfaction among Federal Reserve member banks over the advantages of affiliation with the system has caused the Federal Reserve Bank of New York to make an over-all study of the situation, it was learned yesterday.</br></br>The Federal Reserve Board itself is now believed to be concerned about the problem which has developed largely as a result of the marked disparity between member and non-member banks arising from last year's increases in reserve requirement and the possibility of further increases. McCabe, that increases in requirements should apply as well to non-member insured banks.</br></br>Most of the recent dissatisfaction, of course, has developed outside the New York area, in sections where the immediate question has always been whether the local banks could better be served through membership in the Federal Reserve System than through correspondent banks in the large cities. Now, however, on a purely dollars and .cents basis, the Federal Reserve’s 'representatives concede that the advantages have less weight, especially since the majority of the member banks do not use all of the services which the system ioffers.</br></br>These representatives do maintain, none the less, that the system, operating in the public interest, renders an important service to member and non-member banks alike and that the modern banking structure would be inoperative without the machinery of the Federal Reserve. text: WASHINGTON, Oct. 29—The powers of the President to avert and dispel national emergencies—powers which are made specific in certain statutes and by some persons are asserted to be virtually unlimited by the language of the Constitution—have again become a burning topic. text: ¥our editorial of July 24, “Wages and Prices,” expressed the view that wage increases had aggravated inflation and would prevent price reductions on. the ground that “high consumer in- j comes” make possible “the sale of goods and services at the higher prices required to cover higher costs.” May I make the following qualifications in order that we may have a clearer understanding of the relation between wages and prices ? (1) “High consumer incomes” incident to high money wages do not neces- ] sarily lead to “the sale of goods and services” at higher prices. Since the purchasing power of money wages is inversely related to prices, a further increase in money wages would narrow the existing deflationary gap between the cost of living and consumer incomes. In other words, increased money wages would merely offset a decrease in real wages, and so enable the existing inventories to be taken off the shelves at current prices. This will hold valid as long as money wages lag far behind the cost of living.</br></br>(2) Even if higher wages increase consumer incomes, it does not necessarily follow that inflation will be aggravated. It must be remembered that an increase in money incomes results in increased output rather than increased prices as long as the economy is at less than full employment. That is to say, as long as there are unemployed resources—human and material —to be utilized for increasing production a further increase in aggregate demand will not be dissipated in higher prices but will increase output and employment.</br></br>Although we have an approximation to full employment of labor at present, we are far from full employment of equipment. This means that the American economy is still capable of increasing output with the existing labor supply. When supply can no longer be increased because of full employment of labor and of equipment, as is conceivable at the height of a cyclical boom, then one can cogently argue about the inflationary danger of increased consumer incomes.</br></br>(3) Higher wages do not necessarily increase costs except perhaps in the case of marginal industries. Efficient industries can afford higher wages precisely because their unit costs are low. Even if it is true, as you aver, that wages have increased faster than productivity, and therefore have caused “substantially higher unit labor costs,” it is not a conclusive argument against future wage increases.</br></br>1 that higher productivity is a matter of an optimum combination of factors, including both capital and labor. text: THE United States is proceeding- headlong toward the worst economic crisis of all time. That is the unqualified prediction of Fritz Sternberg, who. unfortunately, is a prophet with a remarkable record for accuracy.</br></br>The introductory portion of this book amounts to a sort of revision, in the light of late history, of the works of Karl Marx and Frederick Engels. Sternberg points out a few miscalculations they detected in their early writings and corrected themselves, as well as a few more miscalculations now apparent to Sternberg and corrected by him. These somewhat tedious chapters should not keep the reader from his highly important and perhaps historical analysis of the immediate fate of this country.</br></br>Although Sternberg leans heavily on the more enduring products of Marx and Engels, he carefully buttresses his observations with such radically different sources — conservatively different sources, rather—as the reports of the Securities and Exchange Commission and the publications of the Brookings Institution.</br></br>The heart of Sternberg's case is based on the acknowledged fact that in the course of World War II the industrial plant of the United States developed so rapidly that it is now able to produce 50 per cent, more goods than in 1940. Obviously, we want to keep right on producing that extra 50 per cent. The Office of War Mobilization and Reconversion declared after Japan surrendered: “We are not seeking to go back to previous levels of employment or output. We are seeking to expand our output rapidly to forty or fifty per cent above former peacetime levels.” This means that, with Government purchase of war materiel dropping off sharply, peacetime sales — consumption—must be increased permanently by 50 per cent. Sternberg believes that we will find this-impossible after the present rosy transition period in which our economy is kept rolling by war-delayed capital investments and by pent-up consumer demands presently met primarily by war savings.</br></br>^ FTER this transition, what? Pessimists believe that post-war plans of the Army and Navy might absorb 10 per cent of our 50 per cent production increase. No optimist believes foreign trade will absorb 10 per cent more. The balance of between 30 per cent and 40 per cent must therefore be absorbed by the people of the United States, and Sternberg holds that this cannot be done unless the total sum of real (not dollar) wages increases by the same 30 per cent to 40 per cent compared to pre-war levels. Is such a wage increase likely? Sternberg states, “I know of no serious publication which dares to suggest that there is any such likelihood.”

text: WASHINGTON, May 24 — Official Washington, confronted with an economy Congress and a developing European economic crisis, is seriously considering a different approach to the problem of European reconstruction.</br></br>The old approach was to deal with the shattered economies of the several nations one at a time, lending now to Britain, then to France, then to Italy, etc. The new approach is based on the; growing conviction that the problems of all these countries are inter-related and that Europe cannot recover by shoring up, one at a time, the various national economies.</br></br>What is under urgent and thoughtful consideration is a proposal to call on the nations of Europe to suggest a more coordinated continental economy < as a preliminary to the United States meeting them with a large-scale program of "continental aid.”</br></br>Thi3 idea is merely in the germinating stage. text: FRENCH LICK. Ind., April 15— Except for scattered "adjustments of excesses,” already under way, there is no evidence that a period of economic recession may be expected at any time in the immediate future, according to a group of top banking executives from sixj key areas of the nation. The bankers, among those attending the executive council sessions of the American Bankers Association here, stated today that the earlier forecasts of certain economic observers that a recession would develop this spring have now been disproven.</br></br>Although conceding that there had been a marked "shakeout” in soft goods lines, the bankers declared that they were unconcerned over the development, and were continuing their own activities in a normal fashion without exercising any more than the usual caution.</br></br>The bankers, whose home areas included the West Coast, the Southwest, the South, the Middle West and New England as well as New York, stated that they had observed no popular fears of recession, although they agreed that greater selectivity on the part of buyers was evident. People, whether farmers, industrialists or consumers* are now taking a more realistic view of prices, demanding a better return for their dollars, but, and perhaps most importantly, there is no actual unwilling-! ness to spend, they said.</br></br>In all areas, it was agreed, sales of consumers’ durable goods are] holding firm, and consumer credit is on the rise. Business loans are also expanding, it was said, and competition among the banks seeking to make loans continues keen in most areas. There is no apparent unemployment problem, the bankers stated, but the wartime shortage of qualified personnel continues.</br></br>While the volume of individual business operations is not to be compared with the wartime peaks, current activity is generally satisfactory, they asserted. Obviously, unless there is to be serious inflation, the wartime price levels must be further adjusted, \yith the con- < sequent deflationary effects, the bankers declared. But the nation : now appears to be moving along ! on a kind of economic plateau, they said, and at present, at least, there is no sign that it will drop off.

text: WASHINGTON, Nov. 12 UP)— The text of Secretary of Commerce Harriman’F statement on foreign aid to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee follows:</br></br>I appreciate the opportunity to appear before this committee today to state my views on one of the most important questions now faced by our country—the problem of whether and to what extent we shall assist in the economic recovery of western Europe. text: The financial-industrial scene last year was a baffling one with conflicting signs of boom and impending recession. '</br></br>The total net income of 823 companies in 1947 amounted to $5,188,534,180 compared with their 1946 return of $3,442,546,965. Making allowance for these changes, it is apparent that demand and prices were principal factors for last year's betterment. Furthermore, industrial plant expansion and modernization programs provided from reserves set up in prior years combined to swell production and earnings last year. A total of $16,000,000,000 was spent on new facilities in 1947, or more than 28 per cent over the amount expended in 1946. There is probably no domestic issue in which more Americans have a direct and personal interest than the one to which the authors of this section refer as that of “present cruelly high prices.” Over and above this consideration, moreover, is the fact that until and unless the forces of inflation can be contained they must be regarded as a continuing threat to that stabilization of the American economy which is so essential to world recovery and world peace.</br></br>There is less room for approbation, unfortunately, in the platform’s analysis of this problem and its program for dealing with it The high cost of living, this section declares, “is due to the fact that the Government has not effectively used the powers it possesses to combat inflation.” Instead, it has “deliberately encouraged higher prices.” As for the Republican party, the platform pledges it to “attack the basic causes of inflation" from these directions: (1) “Progressive reduction of the cost of Government through elimination of waste"; (2) “stimulation of production”; (3) "fiscal policies to provide increased incentive for production and thrift”; (4) "a sound currency,” and (5) “reduction of the public debt.”</br></br>In accusing “the Government" of failure to deal effectively with the inflation problem, the Republicans have reference, presumably, to the period from the termination of the fighting war in 1945 to January, 1947, when the Democrats were still in control of Congress. And there is no doubt that the record of the Administration over those months abundantly warrants such criticism. Mr. Truman elected, at the war’s end, to listen to his New Deal economic advisers (including those closely associated with Henry A. Wallace). These advisers, unhappily, succeeded in convincing him that the nation was headed for deflation and depression unless industry granted wage increases sufficient to restore and maintain labor’s wartime level of “take-home pay.” The President threw the weight of the Administration behind this anti-deflation thesis, and as a result doomed to failure the Administration’s subsequent pathetic efforts at price control. text: WASHINGTON, May 13—Emil Schram, president of the New York Stock Exchange, scouted today the danger of unleashed inflation or disastrous depression and anticipated an accelerated return to lower prices and a competitive era in the national economy.</br></br>In testimony before the Joint Economic Committee studying inflation and bank credit problems, Mr. Schram placed his reliance on voluntary restraint by the public, industrial price reductions and a restricted national budget as pointers to a termination of the period of shortages and the advent of the post-war period of stabilization.</br></br>‘‘Provided we keep our heads,” he told the committee, ‘‘I do not fear runaway inflation nor do I look for the great depression whose failure to appear has so chagrined the Marxian economists and statesmen.”</br></br>Foreseeing additional price cuts, if the third round of wage increases were held to minor proportions, he said: ‘‘We cannot hope to attain absolute stability—it is not part of a dynamic economy. However, if we do not depress business psychology unnecesssarily and adopt voluntary restraints such as the American Bankers Association has advocated, I see no reason why a large volume of goods and services cannot continue to be produced and taken off the market.”</br></br>While deeming it ‘‘folly to expect a return to the pre-war price level, with a $40,000,000,000 Federal budget and a $250,000,000,000 national debt, Mr. Schram contended that ‘‘we have emerged from the period of shortages and unless the Congress permits the budget to become unbalanced again, I firmly believe we have already entered the post-war period of stabilization.”

text: THE agreement on the budget deficit is doomed to failure. All that time and effort were spent debating the wrong problem. The budget deficit is not the cause of our ailing economy, it is a symptom. By focusing on the deficit, our leaders found political accommodation but they did not begin to address the economy’s actual short- or long-term problems, let alone solve them. In fact, the budget agreement could actually make our economic situation worse.</br></br>The United States has probably already entered its ninth postwar recession. Cutting spending or raising taxes — or both — will only slow the economy still more. Fiscal tightening at this time should be deemed a political felony — reckless endangerment of the economy. In addition to taxing away more of our incomes, our elected officials will cause many of us to lose our jobs as the economy slows.</br></br>What got lost in the debate is that both the Federal deficit and total Federal debt are not at emergency levels. Today’s outstanding debt is equal to about 42 percent of our gross national product — not too bad by historical standards. During the post-World War II boom, total debt was gradually brought down from more than 100 percent of G.N.P. immediately after the war to about</br></br>Robert Ortner was Under Secretary of Commerce during the Reagan Administration. He is author of "Voodoo Deficits." 25 percent a decade ago. It was brought down gradually through economic growth and not with debt-reduction measures.</br></br>The United States has been growing at about 2 percent to 2.5 percent or less each year while Japan has been growing at 4 percent to 5 percent. The reason Japan outstrips us in growth is that it allocates a much larger share of its domestic output to research and development and to capital spending than we do. While Japan invests about a quarter of its national income in new plants and equipment, we manage to invest only an eighth. Japan’s investment allocation is highest among the major industrial countries. Ours is the lowest. The inevitable result is that productivity in Japan, especially in manufacturing, is growing more than twice as fast as in the United States.

text: THE economy is growing weaker. The Northeast is in recession. Housing prices are off everywhere. Unemployment is up. Household income is slipping and retail sales are sluggish. But in all this gloom, a few sectors of the economy still hold their own, and chief among them is capital spending.</br></br>Capital spending, the investments that companies make in factories, offices, stores, machinery and other equipment needed to do business, dropped sharply in previous periods of economic weakness. Why invest, corporations reasoned, if people are not buying and profits are endangered? Although such thinking is in evidence today, capital spending continues anyway for a bagful of special reasons.</br></br>One important reason is that the nation’s airlines are spending more than $1.5 billion a month on a new generation of aircraft. Big sums are also going into pollution control and other devices mandated by the Government to protect the environment. The nation’s auto industry is getting help from auto rental and leasing companies, which have bought thousands of vehicles this year. Drilling oil wells, another form of capital spending, was on the rise even before the Middle East crisis, and higher oil prices are encouraging more activity. Spending is now close to $1 billion a month, oil industry data show.</br></br>The biggest sum of all, more than $3 billion a month, is going into office equipment, particularly computers, and these purchases are often made to reduce labor and save on wages. The weak economy itself is stimulating this sort of investment, and so is the memory of the early 1980’s. In those years, severe recession combined with stiff foreign competition left a legacy among American execu- “What endures today is the belief that hard times are no longer short term,” said Martin N. Bailey, a productivity expert at the Brookings Institution. "You are much more in a competitive dogfight than you used to be. So as soon as you get into an economic downturn, you reassess. A recession becomes another justification to lay off people and put in automated equipment.”</br></br>Demographics are also driving the process. With fewer young people available for entry-level low-wage jobs than in the 1970’s and 1980’s, many retailers, for example, are automating these tasks. Companies including J. C. Penney; Sears, Roebuck, and supermarket chains like Giant Foqd are installing sophisticated, electronic cash register and inventory control systems that save on labor. “Companies are seeing that they have to operate with a different-age work force, and therefore they automate,” Mr. Bailey said.

text: Leonard Silk attributes to Edward M. Bernstein, first research director of the International Monetary Fund, the belief that the chronic United States trade deficit with Japan is chiefly the result of the undervaluation of the yen, which represents deliberate Japanese policy (Economic Scene column, Jan. 12). Moreover, Mr. Silk believes this to be part of the reason trade pressure is mounting on the Japanese. I would like to clarify United States-Japan trade issues.</br></br>As for the assertion that the yen is undervalued because of a Japanese policy to purchase billion-dollar bonds, 1 would mention first that the fundamental relationship of international balance of payments components is that the surplus of current balance is equal to the deficit of both capital balance and balance of monetary movements (the amount of inflow of money to Japan must be equal to the outflow). This is not economic theory, but accounting fact.</br></br>Japanese investors have to invest surplus money overseas, but the monetary authority of Japan does not manipulate how or where that money is invested, nor can it influence the investment with regulations or guidelines. Japanese investors are said to have bought West German mark assets and, since the collapse of the Berlin Wall, are starting to shift money from the United States to West Germany. The yen has thus weakened against the mark and become more stable against the dollar in the last two months.</br></br>Political changes aside, one striking feature of the recent past is the dominant influence of nominal interest rate differentials on international capital flows. This has led to the somewhat paradoxical result that countries with deficits, like the United States, with relatively high inflation rates and high interest rates, have experienced large-scale capital inflows, which have put upward pressure on their exchange rates. Countries with surpluses, like Japan, have the reverse effects. Such situations produce clear risks.</br></br>there is a strong possibility that current-account imbalances will worsen and that unsustainable foreign investment levels will give rise to serious policy dilemmas and disturbances in financial markets. To counter these risks, the Japanese Monetary Authority is monitoring and acting in the foreign exchange market in close contact with other countries in the monetary Group of Seven (the United States, Britain, France, West Germany, Italy and Canada). To cut trade imbalances, we must keep in mind the basic relationship, which is also the accounting fact, that the difference between a country’s exports and imports is exactly equal to the difference between its savings and investments. In recent bilateral talks, the United States focused on such Japanese problems as the tendency to save a lot, but not invest enough on infrastructure, an inefficient distribution system and business practices that exclude newcomers. Japan responded with its list: the American tendency to consume a lot, but not save enough, lack of emphasis on exporting, inadequate worker education, business practices that focus on short-term profits, rather than long-term productivity.

In this case, the high-pressure tactics used against bondholders are very similar to those used against stockholders in the 1960’s — before the adoption of Securities and Exchange Commission rules for stock tender offers.</br></br>To combat these tactics, the S.E.C. needs to extend its rules on stock tender offers to bond tender offers. This is the main thrust of a rule-making petition filed with the S.E.C. by Fidelity Investments and the Prudential Insurance Company. The petition focuses on tender offers by troubled companies to buy back their bonds at deep discounts — $30 to $40, say, for a $100 bond — through high-pressure tactics that effectively deprive the bondholders of their right to make an informed choice.</br></br>While the management of a troubled company should be allowed to restructure its outstanding debt in order to avoid bankruptcy, bondholders deserve a fair opportunity to negotiate the terms of the restructuring. Under current S.E.C. rules, however, bondholders are denied most of the rights granted stockholders.</br></br>When someone makes a tender offer to the shareholders of a public company, the same price must be offered to each and every shareholder. By contrast, a company may offer to buy bonds from only a selected group of bondholders, or may simultaneously offer to buy bonds at different prices from different groups of bondholders. The S.E.C. should prohibit such discriminatory practices by applying its “offer to all” and “same consideration” rules to bond tender offers.

text: CHANGES in the spread between short-term and long-term interest rates may be the best means of forecasting business-cycle turning points. When short rates are lower than long — as they are now — the economy tends to grow. But when long rates drop below short, recession looms.</br></br>Over the last 25 years, movements in the "term structure" of interest rates, or yield curve, have correctly predicted all the major peaks and troughs in the United States business cycle, according to Prof. Campbell R. Harvey of Duke University’s Fuqua School of Business.</br></br>Unlike other indicators, the yield curve has put out no false signals. In the third quarter of 1968, the curve began an inversion, changing its slope from positive to negative, and correctly signaled the recession of 1969-70, which started five months after long rates dropped below short rates.</br></br>The yield curve inverted two months before the 1973-75 recession began. In the fourth quarter of 1978 and in the fourth quarter of 1980, the yield curve inverted, recovered and inverted again, correctly predicting the double-dip recessions of 1980 and 1981-82, which some economists see as one recession.</br></br>How about the latest recession, which may or may not be over? The Administration attributed the onset of the recession to the outbreak of the Persian Gulf crisis in August 1990. But the inversion of the yield curve in the second quarter of 1989 had predicted the downturn that began five months later — the average lag between inversions and recessions.

text: IT is an article of faith in financial markets that lower interest rates are good for the economy and higher rates are bad.</br></br>But goodness and badness depend on the financial condition of the beholder. text: Robert B. Reich makes some good points in “How Business Can Help in Schools" (Forum, June 9), but his recommendation that business should give large sums of money to public elementary and secondary schools misses the point about our educational failures.</br></br>Schools don’t work because they are monopolies. They will not become better if they are given a few more dollars either through the tax system or through gifts. Would Mr. Reich urge that American corporations give money to Soviet factories in their present socialist system in order to make the factories succeed? These “adopt-a-school” programs to get business to give money to public schools are as absurd as trying to solve the problems of the postal service by urging each local business to “adopt-a-post-office." What the schools need is deregulation, competition and market incentives, not more dollars poured into a failed socialist system.</br></br>The eight points delineated in ‘‘How Business Can Help in Schools,” are on target. May I add three more: 1. Because most of the important decisions about schooling are made at the local level, corporate employees, especially managers, should become more knowledgeable about their local school boards, attend board meetings and commit to a three- to five-year term as a school board member.</br></br>2. Corporate employees, especially managers, should be encouraged to find out about the vocational-educational programs in their home communities. If they are merely “holding bins," then work to encourage improved modem programming designed to educate tomorrow’s workers. Take time to serve as a volunteer on the “craft committees” or advisory boards which assist vocational schools in staying current in curriculum and techniques.</br></br>3. Working alone, or with others, many Chambers of Commerce have education subcommittees that assist local school districts — encourage employees to volunteer as mentors, speakers or models for “shadowing" programs that enable youngsters to learn about individuals’ jobs by following them for a day.

text: THIS has been a tough year for free-marketeers in Washington, who find themselves trying to explain why the United States is practically the only major industrial power without a cohesive industrial policy. And while at times it suffers from superficiality and a strangely benevolent view of authoritarian regimes, it has a lot to say about how nations keep their eyes on the ball.</br></br>What makes the so-called four dragons such important topics of study these days is that, in the years leading up to the war in Vietnam, they were the dominoes supposedly waiting to fall. But while none of them became Communist, none of them chose capitalism either — at least not in the American sense. Instead, they turned to various forms of the Japanese model — what one Singapore official terms “capitalism with socialist characteristics.”</br></br>Though American economists tend to lump the four dragons together as very similar economies, and by implication similar societies, Mr. Vogel is at his best when he describes what different economic animals they really are. Almost half a century after the end of World War II. he writes, the</br></br>Korean relationship with the Japanese is “not ‘love and hate’ but ‘respect and hate.’ ” Yet Korea, more than any other country in the region, has mimicked the Japanese system. text: I read “The Family Business — Letting Go” (Your Own Account, Jan. 5) with great interest. But we need to look deeper at the succession dilemma.</br></br>Why do entrepreneurs and many business owners hate to plan? Very often, their psyche loathes structure and accountability. Like a modern-day Indiana Jones, they relish “making it up as they go along,” lurching from project to project. The more fundamental issue is, “what’s the goal of all this effort?” Am I creating a nourishing vehicle for future generations or does my ego tell me to die in the saddle? Are my family members better off? Do they matter?</br></br>During the succession process, generations of family dysfunctions come home to roost. Unless those are untangled, there is little hope for moving into the next generation. Some succession plans even institutionalize unresolved family conflict. Plan or no plan, incompetent heirs, unrealistic expectations of entitlement, alcoholism, addictive behaviors, fears of retirement, conditional love and even genetics play a part in the succession drama.</br></br>Well families beget well family businesses. Well families glide through the succession process, with or without a plan. I came to this conclusion reluctantly, as traditional business education supports the notion that business behavior is rational, mutually supportive, and principally seeks to increase return on investment. Many family businesses have none of these characteristics.</br></br>There is great joy when families in business act in harmony. And there can be no greater satisfaction for a parent than to pass on his or her legacy to a child. Succession is a long, intensely personal process, requiring an openness at every step of the way. When family business owners are open to their family needs, acknowledge their limitations and focus on a goal, succession works.

text: With interest rates falling to levels that haven’t been seen for decades, more homeowners are applying for home equity loans to consolidate other types of consumer debt. There are two reasons for the popularity of these loans, which are just ordinary second mortgages despite their trendy name.</br></br>First, the rates on home equity loans are much lower than those on other types of consumer debt like credit card balances, car loans and personal loans. Second, with the phase-out of interest deductions for most other types of consumer loans, home equity loans are the only type of tax-deductible consumer borrowing except for regular home mortgages.</br></br>There are two types of home equity loans. With an open-end loan, you can have access to a line of credit secured by your house. You typically borrow the funds as you need them, up to the maximum loan amount approved, by writing a check or draft. The loan has a variable interest rate that is linked to the prime lending rate the bank charges its most creditworthy corpo- rate customers; the rate usually is 1(4 to U/2 percentage points above prime. With a closed-end loan, you borrow a specific amount for a set period of time, generally 5 to 10 years, and the interest rate is generally higher than with an open-end loan.</br></br>To obtain a home equity loan, you must have accumulated a significant amount of equity — that is, your cash down payment plus any paid-down balance on your first mortgage — in your home. Many lenders limit borrowing to 75 percent of a home’s current value. Assume, for example, that you recently purchased a home for $100,000, borrowing $75,000 and making a $25,000 cash down payment.</br></br>If your bank had a 75 percent loan-to-value ratio, you would not be able to obtain a home equity loan because your current mortgage of $75,000 would already represent 75 percent of the home’s current value. text: Why, exactly, did stocks unravel Tuesday afternoon, with the Dow industrials losing 91 points, mainly in the last hour? No one really knew. There was the usual doubletalk about “support levels” and “corrections,” but the only reasonable explanation seemed to be that investors suddenly grasped the idea that with interest rates rising, they could get better yields in bonds. If so, they were a bit slow on the uptake — it had been a full week since the Federal Reserve gave its latest shove to rates. There was also talk that weakness in "cyclical” stocks — the ones that rely on a strong economy — yanked the wider market down. But a lot of it is probably just trigger-happy traders: no economy is as bumpy as this market. Sure enough, on Wednesday the market steadied, and on Fri-day the few traders who showed up sent the Dow to a 33-point rebound.</br></br>Bob Dole certainly got the capital-gains stew bubbling again. Last week he threatened, briefly, to withhold his support for a world trade pact unless President Clinton came around on this much-debated issue. Cutting the gains tax, now 28 percent, is dear to Republican hearts — it’s part of their “Contract With America.” But would it be just another tax lollipop for the rich? No, some say: with the rate high, the rich just sit on stale assets, tying up capital that could invigorate new ventures. And after a capital-gains cut, they say, tax revenue would flood into the Treasury. Then again, if politicians just left the tax alone, nobody would wait for the political winds to shift; they’d sell assets when the time seemed right. But of course politicians can’t leave things alone — they’d be out of a job.</br></br>No one suggests letting the poor go without medical care, but a lot of people are struggling to find a way to cut costs. And preventive care is cheaper than letting someone get really sick and land in a hospital emergency room. On that theory, presumably. New Jersey officials proposed last week to cut Medicaid payments to hospitals by 20 percent. “We cannot be in the business of subsidizing hospitals,” a state official said. That makes sense — but the state has only just begun to arrange preventive-care alternatives. Can hospitals absorb such cutbacks yet? *</br></br>Who owns mutual savings banks, anyway? More to the point, if they're sold, who should profit? Some insist that depositors own them, and should get any windfall. In reality, bank executives have often cut nice deals for themselves, getting stock and options worth millions during sales — rewards earned, they say, for their long service. But last week Federal regulators clamped down: no free stock, no options. They did back down on one issue. Outside investors have put money in banks to qualify as depositors when the payoff came, and regulators had considered limiting insider rights to local depositors — but relented after some investors sued.</br></br>There’s not much left to believe in. Politicians keep disappointing, rumors persist that Santa Claus doesn’t exist, and now even the Pentium chip, that pinnacle of high technology, is less than perfect. Even as computers are vilified for running our lives, they are also seen as islands of precision in an imprecise world. But once in a long while, it seems, the Pentium — which is made by Intel and is in perhaps 10 percent of all personal computers sold — makes a slight division error. Intel — which has fixed it and is offering replacements-, though not a recall — insists that a typical user would have just one chance in nine billion of an error. For some, that’s too risky. And anyway, did Intel use a Pentium to calculate that risk?

text: THE Federal Reserve is supposed to smooth capitalism's bumps. Its track record, however, has been oddly one-sided. When the economy is booming, the Fed is very good at slowing it down — reducing inflation but also making it harder for people to buy homes, keep jobs and purchase cars. Then, a funny thing happens once the economy slows: The Fed gets reluctant to bring back prosperity.</br></br>That reluctance is very much in evidence now. Until February, the economy was robust. The Fed’s response, given its visceral hatred of inflation, was to slow it down by doubling interest rates in the space of a year. The slowdown came, and the urgency to act disappeared, although by law the Fed is supposed to be as quick to maintain jobs as to control inflation.</br></br>The public does not know what the policymakers — 15 men and three women — are saying in their current closed-door deliberations over whether to lower interest rates. But now we know what they were saying the last time the economy reached a peak and then slowed sharply, which was in 1989. The pattern then was eerily similar to 1995, even to the month — February — when the policymakers decreed their last rate increase. And now the Fed, hewing to the practice of releasing transcripts with a five-year delay, has recently made public the 1989 transcripts. They offer a rare, fly-on-the-wall view of how Fed policymakers behave during a turning point in the economy.</br></br>The details are different, then and now. The inflation rate was higher in 1989, for example, than it is today. Real estate was more of a drag on the economy, junk bonds were a problem, and wages seemed more likely to rise, contributing to inflation. But by all accounts, the dialogue and the dynamics of dealing with a slowing economy are strikingly similar. And seven of the 1989 policymakers are still there, starting with Alan Greenspan, the chairman.</br></br>that the calls I’ve made and the data that I’ve looked at suggest that there is a much broader softening out there than 1 think I perceived at [our last] meeting,” he said during a telephone conference call on May 31. Instead, just two months later on June 5, Mr. Greenspan ordered the first cut in rates. It was just a quarter-point decline, and he and his colleagues kept lowering rates bit by bit for the next three yeats. text: FORT WORTH. July 2 — Not so long ago, American workers would suffer the sting of a recession by losing jobs or having their hours or wages reduced. text: ECONOMICS — a relative latecomer to the modern social sciences — has frequently had occasion to revel in the stature it has achieved. The President has no Council of Sociological Advisers, and there is no Nobel laureate in psychology or history. Economists are everywhere sought after, called upon by governments, corporations and the news media to impart meaning to what so often seems frightening and confusing — from our declining wages and stagnating productivity to our endless trade and budget deficits. So why does economics as a profession seem under siege?</br></br>A recent study by the American Economic Association, for example, found that nearly two-thirds of graduate economics professors consider their calling “overly mathematical” and “too unrelated to the real world.” The number of Americans earning Ph.D.’s in economics has fallen by almost half in the past 20 years, to barely 400 a year.</br></br>In universities, the field of economics exists in a fractious state labeled — for want of a better term — “post-Keynesian,” akin to the oddly drifting larger world we’ve come to call “post-Communist.” As in the external world, a divisive fundamentalism seems rife. There are the old advocates of neoclassical synthesis, monetarists, new classicals, neo- and post-Keynesians, neo-institutionalists, supply-siders and several variant Marxists — a cacophony, in short, in a profession that for the preceding 40 years had effectively spoken in one voice.</br></br>But why? The explanation by Robert Heilbroner and William Milberg in “The Crisis of Vision in Modern Economic Thought” may be the most imaginative to date. It is, they argue in this disarmingly challenging little book, what they term "a crisis of vision.”</br></br>For Mr. Heilbroner, the Norman Thomas Professor of Economics, Emeritus, at the New School for Social Research, and Mr. Milberg, an assistant professor of economics at the New School, vision is neither a religious nor a mystical experience. It is what Joseph Schumpeter 40 years ago identified in his commanding “History of Economic Analysis” as a pre-analytic, pre-theoretical grasp of the central issues each great period in economics is meant to address. Possessed of such vision, economics enters what Mr. Heilbroner and Mr. Milberg call “classical situations,” extended historical moments when the richness of the central vision gives rise to industrious reflection and analysis that fills out the vision and gives it both power and meaning for its particular age.

text: The Census Bureau reported last week that households have recaptured the income they lost in the recession of the early 90’s. But to sustain that level of income, more and more people had to work in full-time jobs, especially women.</br></br>THE Census Bureau announced last week that the median income of American households rose in 1996 for the third year in a row, even after allowing for inflation. At last, the economic expansion appears to be lifting a lot of boats. Certainly the Clinton Administration says so. After years of stagnant incomes, the President said, "America’s middle class, no longer forgotten, is rising fast.” But there’s a less sanguine explanation buried in the Census report and in other Government data. Fathers and mothers, sons and daughters are working longer hours for roughly the same hourly pay. It is not higher wages but extra time on the job that is the main source of the, rising household income. That is a precarious affluence. When the economy weakens, as it inevitably will, the extra work can disappear abruptly, as it did in the aftermath of the last recession. Raises are harder to reverse.</br></br>style. But. starting in 1982, the trend reversed and the time devoted to work has risen ever since, apparently accelerating in the 1990’s. Just why is not clear, but a major reason — apart from supplementing skimpy raises — may be job insecurity, according to two economists researching the .trend. Like bears gorging themselves in antici-' pation of winter, American workers are taking on work in these good times to offset the bad years they have been conditioned to expect. “Companies are offering the work, and people are self-insuring themselves, taking all the hours they can get because they are not sure they will have hours next year,” said Barry Bluestone, a labor economist at the University of Massachusetts.</br></br>Mixing data from several sources, Mr. Bluestone and Steven Rose, a senior economist at the Educational Testing Service and a former Labor Department official in the Clinton Administration, found that for workers between 25 and 54, the average number of hours worked rose to 1,980 a year in 1995 from 1,840 in 1982. text: THIS column was supposed to have covered a clever new product, but the clever new product wasted most of my day in a futile attempt to get just one of its features to work. text: Analysts usually make sober, solemn pronouncements in a desperate attempt to make sense of the wild craps game that is the stock market. “Profit-taking,” they intone. “A solid economy.” “Rate fears.” “A correction looms.” Then the market, ignoring them all, goes on its giddy way. But last week — with the Dow up 143 on Monday, down 139 on Wednesday, up 130 at one point on Thursday, and closing the week at 7,169 — one analyst wisely cast solemnity aside. “It reminds me of a cartoon,” said Melissa Brown of Prudential Securities. “Everybody rushes to the side of the ship, and it tilts one way. And then everybody rushes to the other side, and it tilts the other way.” A bit of seasickness is a whole lot better than a cold swim.</br></br>Some mutual fund managers are like status-crazy overachievers in an upper-middle-class neighborhood. If the neighbors get a top-of-the-line Mercedes and a snazzy home theater, they’ve got to have them, too. If the fund next door is riding some hot stock to the stratosphere, no self-respecting fund manager dares sit it out. Bre-X Minerals of Canada was custom-made to set managers’ pulses racing: it had reported a huge gold strike in Indonesia, and its stock price was outdazzling the sun. Mutual funds lapped it up, giving Bre-X shares a market value of $4 billion last year. The punch line, of course: no gold, or at least none worth mining. And the fantasy collapsed last week, leaving Bre-X shares worthless, fund managers red-faced, and investors poorer but, presumably, wiser.</br></br>Britain, which used to own much of the world, is rejoining it. An oversimplification, of course, but that’s basically what Tony Blair, the newly elected Prime Minister, did last week by shifting power over interest rates to the central bank. That’s what many countries do, or are moving to do, for one simple reason: when politicians control interest rates, one of the mightiest economic tools around, they might be tempted by short-term thoughts — say, about the next election. text: CONCORD, N.H., Nov. 30 — AI Gore used to be a stick-to-the-script kind of guy. Lots of mind-numbing facts about the gross domestic product. But since he revamped his campaign two months ago after a slide in the polls, Mr. Gore has also revamped himself and thrown out the script of his standard stump speech.</br></br>Now, the vice president is trying to appeal to real people by portraying himself as a real person, too. He does not make full-blown speeches; he chats. He wanders into living rooms to talk with 30 people or into school gymnasiums to talk with 300 and conducts Oprah-style discussions, which he calls open meetings. He sometimes relies on stock answers to convey his positions on the issues: He wants to resubmit the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty that the Senate recently rejected. He wants to bring “revolutionary change” to public schools. He wants to give health insurance to all children. [Excerpts, Page A28.]</br></br>But more often than not, the message is about him. He talks about being a grandfather, about having lived in a trailer park, about how much he likes the pop singer Ricky Martin. And the medium of open meetings is an important part of the message — that Mr. Gore is open, not the android of his reputation but a confident, freewheeling guy, able to handle any topic thrown at him, able to relate to all kinds of people.</br></br>The result is a scene like one on Tuesday at a high school here, where he was asked about violence, on television. Mr. Gore said he liked to watch “The Simpsons,” prompting a round of applause from the teenage audience. Then he talked about watching the Simpsons watch “The Itchy and Scratchy Show,” the cartoon within the cartoon, with its parody of violence. “They’ll take out a chain saw and slice the arms off, horrible, blood spurting out, and Bart and Lisa and the little baby, Maggie, they’ll laugh and giggle at this mayhem,” he says, laughing himself.</br></br>A1 Gore does not give full-blown speeches, preferring to speak before smaller groups, like this gathering last month at a school in Nashua, N.H.

text: Surely among the other qualities that distinguished the career of Isaac Bashevis Singer, who won the Nobel Prize in 1978, was his capacity for seemingly endless productivity. If that is the case, why?</br></br>It happens that I gave “Shadows on the Hudson” what is commonly considered a rave review. Indeed, a critic in a review that has yet to appear deems “Shadows” a failure that should not have been published at all. I do not agree, but I have been wondering whether, paradoxically. Singer felt the same way as the less generous critics, especially about the book’s not being published.</br></br>And so another question: Could it be that the very qualities of the book that fed Singer’s ambivalence are the same that led me to find this final opus so extraordinary? “Shadows on the Hudson” follows two years in the lives of a group of tempestuously anguished Jewish survivors who live in New York City not long after the Holocaust shattered their lives. The Forward presented it in twice-weekly installments in the late 1950’s.</br></br>It wasn’t until two decades or so later thdt Singer gained his large and adoring English-language following, at which point he devoted a great deal of his effort to editing his earlier Yiddish works and preparing them for translation and publication. text: It’s summer, and another flock of recent high-school graduates is about to head off to the college of their dreams. The question now is how they'll pay for it. text: HOME buyers shopping for a loan this summer will find that for the first time in two years a fixed-rate mortgage is perhaps a more attractive option than an adjustable-rate mortgage. The reasons are a decline in long-term interest rates and tighter guidelines at the Federal National Mortgage Association, or Fannie Mae, over what type of adjustable-rate loans it will buy from lenders.</br></br>In the first half of June, the average interest rate nationally on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage was 9.98 percent, down more than one percentage point from March, according to the Federal National Mortgage Association. By comparison, the average adjustable-rate mortgage nationally was 8.96 percent, down only about one-half of a percentage point in the same period.</br></br>Over the last four years, particularly in expensive regions such as the Northeast and California, the adjustable-rate mortgage has been extremely popular because its low initial rate translates into a lower monthly payment. That feature has allowed many home buyers to qualify for loans they could not have afforded if they had higher, fixed rates. The loans are also attractive because they generally require a lower down payment.</br></br>But whenever home buyers can justify the higher initial cost of a fixed-rate loan, they frequently do so because they prefer its stability.</br></br>In the summer of 1987, lenders were swamped with applications for fixed-rate home loans and refinancings when the interest rate on many of the loans dropped below 10 percent, an important psychological barrier. text: WASHINGTON, March 21 — When the Government’s report on producer prices hit the news wires last Friday morning, many economists figured that the Federal Reserve would have no alternative but to slam the econ- medicine. text: LONDON, Nov. 14 — President-elect Bush will find his West European allies uncertain about two things when he begins meeting with them in Washington this week: how he intends to reduce the American budget deficit, and how the alliance should respond to rapid change in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe.</br></br>Of the two issues, the second poses by far the more difficult challenge, in the view of diplomats and Government officials here and in Washington.</br></br>On the need to reduce the $150 billion budget deficit, Chancellor Helmut Kohl of West Germany, who will see Mr. Bush on Tuesday, and Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher of Britain, who follows on Thursday, both agree — though neither is likely to presume to offer Mr. Bush a prescription for doing it.</br></br>Their advisers and diplomats say they will try to persuade him that the European Community’s moves to eliminate internal trade and tariff barriers by the end of 1992 do not constitute a threat to the United States. Both will encourage him to fight protectionist pressures from Congress to reduce the trade deficit by raising American tariffs on imported goods.</br></br>This much the allies are agreed on. Where they do not agree is on questions like these: Is the threat from the Soviet Union so much reduced that NATO can forgo modernizing some weapons sys- terns, or relax its curbs against exporting Western technology to Moscow? Do Mr. Gorbachev’s policies mean greater stability in Eastern Europe, or greater instability, and how should NATO prepare in either case? And how can Europe count on the United States for its defense if Washington lowers the budget deficit — and military spending ■ at the same time?

text: INVESTORS who try to predict the stock market’s direction by studying such fundamentals as corporate earnings and interest rates are not alone in their current confusion. Fundamental Assumption Adopted</br></br>In conducting our analysis, we have adopted the fundamental assumption that extreme price volatility, such as occurred during the market break, Is undesirable. text: THE first time Robert R. Glauber saw room 1116 at the Federal Reserve building in New York, it depressed him. That day in early November the big room where he would spend the next two months had one chair in it, one desk and one telephone.</br></br>President Reagan had just appointed Nicholas F. text: In four intense days of hearings before the Senate Banking Committee, representatives of the Federal Reserve Board, the Securities and Exchange Commission, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the New York Stock Exchange and other experts differed on how to prevent any future collapses on Wall Street. But a surprising number of their proposals had essentially one purpose: to reduce, though not eliminate, gyrations in slock prices.</br></br>Higher margins, predesignated trading halts, price limits, program-trading limits like those the Stock Exchange voted on Thursday — all are aimed at stopping the wild price fluctuations that sent investors running to liquidate their positions last fall.</br></br>No one made the point with more understatement than the S.E.C. staff. “In conducting our analysis," its report said, “we have adopted the fundamental assumption that extreme price volatility, such as occurred during the market break, is undesirable.”</br></br>Even the most ardent frec-market thinkers agreed that something had to be done about volatility. “Price limits and other circuit breakers must be viewed as inherently destabilizing," Alan Greenspan, chairman of the Federal Reserve, told the committee. “But they may be the least bad of all the solutions.” Saying that volatility is bad may seem axiomatic, but the obvious masks a difficult balance that free market economists and regulators have to reach. They want to institute new trading rules that dampen price swings enough to restore investor confidence, while avoiding burdensome regulations that add new costs and inefficiencies to the nation’s capital markets and drive trading overseas. Not only would that diminish the United States as the world's financial center, but it would inevitably make it more costly for American corporations to raise new money for investment in plant and equipment.</br></br>The regulators and members of Congress agree that any basic changes in regulation of the stock, bond and futures markets will be gradual, but many feel they have lime. Most predict that the Dow Jones industrial average, having fallen 508 points Oct. 19, is not about to take another plunge. Besides that, they believe that the relationship between the stock market and the health of the overall American economy is loose enough that no economic crisis is imminent.

The New York Stock Exchange restricted program trading activity on Tuesday, Oct. 20, to avoid overloading the exchange's order system. The Dow Jones average rebounded 7.8 percent from Tuesday's close Thursday, Nov. 5. On Friday, Nov. 6, the exchange announced that program traders would be permitted to resume activities. They probably have enough statistical evidence to demonstrate that the program traders’ alibis for the events of Oct. 19 are legitimate. Moreover, there must be some attempt to explain to the public that program trading serves a very useful role in the stock market, contrary to Mr. Volcker’s view and the circumstantial evidence mentioned above.</br></br>During the recent emotional collapse of stock prices, the distinction between two types of computer program trading has been blurred. Two of the more popular techniques that take place under this generic term are stock index arbitrage and what is known as portfolio insurance. Stock index arbitrage is simple. On a computer screen, the trader monitors the difference or ‘‘spread’’ between the average value of the 500 Standard & Poor’s stocks traded in New York and the financial futures index traded in Chicago and keyed to the price index of the S.& P. 500 basket of stocks.</br></br>Clearly, such program trading can move the prices of the stocks traded on the New York Stock Exchange. But the impact is always short in duration because the computers facilitate rapid arbitrage transactions. Prices of individual stocks in the program basket can rise or fall by a few points until the discrepancy between Chicago and New York prices is closed.

text: NEMPLOYMENT RATES have been a puzzling indicator of economic health in the Rocky Mountain West during the last year. In Idaho, Montana, Wyoming and Colorado the number of people out of work has dropped, but state labor specialists do not call the change an improvement. Meanwhile, Utah’s unemployment rate inched upward to 6.6 percent in August, though John Mathews of the Utah Depart- “We don’t have statistics to back us up, but we suspect the drop in Idaho’s unemployment is due to outmigration and frusta-tion,” says James Day, research director for the Department of Idaho Employment. This theory seems to hold in the other mountain states where unemployment rates have fallen. In Idaho unemployment has gone from 6.4 percent in August 1986 to 5.3 percent at the end of last summer. “People have just quit looking for jobs,” says Mr. Day.</br></br>“The signs in Utah have been most encouraging,” says Mr. Mathews, who cites “the highest growth in three years in the goods-producing sector.” Of particular note are the primary metals, aerospace and food manufacturing sectors, according to Mr. Mathews.</br></br>Extractive industries such as oil and gas remain depressed, though the number of oil rigs operating in Wyoming is up to 54, an increase of 20 over a year ago. “But there aren’t any real bright spots here,” says Gordon Wolford, a state statistical analyst. “There’s virtually no residential construction, and statewide real-estate prices are down about 30 percent.” The exception is Teton County in northwest Wyoming, where Grand Teton National Park and part of Yellowstone National Park are situated. Tourism has remained strong in Jackson Hole, as has the housing market, Mr. Wolford said.</br></br>In Montana, the agriculture sector improved, and is expected to continue to do well because of an increase in beef and grain prices, according to Kathy Shen-kle, a research specialist with the Department of Labor and Industry. "For ranchers, 1986 was a record year after a few very bad years,” says Ms. Shenkle. “We just don’t know whether the income will circulate in the state and generate new growth, or be used to pay off old debts.”</br></br>In Colorado, the secondary effects of recession have been severe. In a Maine autumn, Arnold set out to cross a wilderness with inaccurate maps and insufficient supplies. It was a good time for foliage but not much else.</br></br>Such was the endurance of his men that, to Mr. Milliman, they were more than human. text: SUDDENLY last week, shortly before his departure for the economic summit conference in Venice, President Reagan announced that Paul A. Volcker had resigned as chairman of the Federal Reserve Board. His successor, Mr. Reagan said, would be Alan Greenspan, a business consultant who served as chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers under Presidents Nixon and Ford.</br></br>Mr. Volcker was widely regarded as the Hercules who slew the Hydra of inflation and as an intrepid defender of the dollar, so as soon as the news of his departure broke Tuesday morning, the bond market, the stock market and the dollar plummeted. Within hours, however, all recovered as the markets decided that Mr. Greenspan would take up the fight against inflation where Mr. Volcker had left off: Pragmatist had replaced pragmatist, conservative had replaced conservative.</br></br>But the arrival of Greenspan and the departure of Volcker, as the smart money sees it, is no simple case of Tweedledum replacing Tweedledee. Banking deregulator has replaced banking regulator. Free-market true believer has replaced intervener. And Republican has replaced Democrat, and a ferociously independent-minded Democrat at that.</br></br>By all accounts, the Reagan camp believed that Republicans and their candidate for the White House might face a serious problem in 1988 if Mr. Volcker stayed. Even at the risk of a recession on the eve of the election, he was fully capable of deciding that an increase in interest rates was needed to block inflation. This was not just an academic possibility: The Reagan Administration, while taking credit for killing inflation, blamed Mr. Volcker’s inflationkilling policies for the severity of the recession of 1981-82. And it remembered that Mr. Volcker’s tough monetary policy of 1979 had choked off economic growth in 1980 and helped drive Jimmy Carter from the White House. Mr. Reagan hesitated to reappoint him, without some evidence that Mr. Volcker would be willing to bend the knee to White House and T reasury guidance.</br></br>But since his toughness and stubborn independence were the very qualities that had made Mr. Volcker a hero to the financial markets and to foreign governments, the Administration also hesitated to dump him.

text: Hasn’t The Times left out a significant part of Paul Volcker’s record in its appraisals since the announcement of the Federal Reserve Board chairman's impending retirement? “An intrepid defender of the dollar” (Week in Review, June 7) is a title not borne out by Mr. Volcker’s role as President Nixon’s Under Secretary of the Treasury in 1971. There, as Secretary John Connally’s principal adviser on monetary affairs, he lent strong support to our country’s breach of the Bretton Woods agreement.</br></br>That agreement pledged its signatories to keep their currencies within a narrow fixed range of their “par” value, and had maintained that system since 1944. It prevented “floating” dollars, pounds, yen, marks, etc.</br></br>In 1971, as now, the United States was running a balance-of-payments deficit: some $13 billion, which by comparison to the $150-$165 billion deficit of recent years seems small. Secretary Connally took steps that he and President Nixon apparently believed would remedy the situation: devalue the dollar by 10 percent, and then let the value of the dollar “float." Mr, Volcker was the Under Secretary for Monetary Affairs, and the expert supporter of this policy.</br></br>Does that remind you of the 1986 steps to devalue the “strong” dollar with which our present Treasury Sec- retary has been identified? text: EVERY lending institution around wants to give you a mortgage these days. The problem is trying to figure out which offers the best deal. text: Everybody knows that inflation erodes the real value of money, right? That it would take, say, about three dollars today to buy the goods and services that a single dollar bought in 1966. Everybody knows this, right? No, wrong. According to Robert Eisner — who is the William R. Kenan Professor of Economics at Northwestern University and a member of the editorial boards of several major economic journals — the people who keep track of the Federal deficit don’t know it.</br></br>As Mr. Eisner argues in “How Real Is the Federal Deficit?”, the people who measure our current annual deficits at around $200 billion and our gross national debt as “approaching to $2 trillion” have failed to make allowances for inflation. If only they would, as Mr. Eisner and his colleague Paul J. Pieper have done, they would discover, for instance, that as recently as 1980 the annual budget deficit was a small percentage of Gross National Product compared with certain other years since 1940. Or that during the Carter Administration, the apparent budget deficits were actually a surplus. Or that from 1945 to the end of 1980, “the real market value of the net federal debt (in constant 1972 dollars) declined’' by $327 billion, “a drop of no less than 58 percent.”</br></br>The implications of this insight are quite staggering, and suggest that the recent economic past has been wholly misread. For instance, Mr. Eisner argues, the Carter Administration’s tightened fiscal policies were misguided because in fact “we did not have real Federal budget deficits from 1977 to 1980.” For instance, the miracle of Reaganomics is not that supply-side economics worked, but that a combination of lower taxes and higher defense spending produced budget deficits that served to stimulate the economy and produce recovery. In short, what Mr. Eisner is driving at is that once we allow for inflation, we see that the Keynesian revolution was never to be questioned; deficit spending has worked all along.</br></br>Can it possibly be so simple? After all the hullabaloo over supply-side economics and the anti-Keynesian, neoclassical revolution, can it really just have been a matter of a missing dollar index? Is David A. Stockman’s hue and cry irrelevant? Actually, it isn’t all that simple, at least as Robert Eisner handles it. His analysis is often extremely difficult to follow. He presents page upon page of complex tables and does several chapters of rigorous statistical analysis. His language is often opaque, even by the standards of a typical economics text.</br></br>And the conclusions he draws are often far from obvious. For instance, he tries to prove that the expansionary effect of adjusted deficits on output as a whole “is such that, widespread belief to the contrary notwithstanding, deficits are positively associated with private investment.” We have “crowding in” rather than “crowding out.” He believes that while “our deficits prove a balance-of-trade drag on our economy, they correspondingly stimulate the economies of other nations." He even finds that increases in deficits “turn out to be associated with increases in Dow Jones stock averages.”

text: MINE years ago David Hand started making folk art, as he is not too self-conscious to call his handcrafted willow furniture. Recession had stilled his construction business, and a divorce had left him in debt. “I was down to $6 and half a tank of gas,” he said. So he headed into the North Alabama hills, as his father had done half a century earlier on similar missions, and hauled back enough swamp willow to make a love seat and two chairs. He sold them for $50 and recalled gratefully, “It bought a lot of groceries.” Now a three-piece set goes for $1,200, and the 56-year-old Mr. Hand’s hardship handiwork can be seen at the best addresses. Including the Governor’s Mansion and the Birmingham Museum of Art. His chairs, settees, tables and headboards consist of slender willow twigs or "benders,” nailed around a sturdy frame. The fluidity of the designs seems to defy the sturdiness of the wood. And as proof that rustic does not have to mean rough, Mr. Hand likes to challenge women to sit in his chairs "with their hose on.”</br></br>Twig furniture such as his originated in the Adirondacks during the mid-to-late-19th century, and came south through the Appalachians, according to Bryding Henley, curator of decorative arts at the Birmingham Museum, which bought one of Mr. Hand’s love seats. "It is surprising that his is so similar to the Adirondack furniture,” says Mrs. Henley. "David’s work is of that quality and yet he developed his style on his own. I think he’s probably the best in the South.”</br></br>Just because Mr. Hand’s letterhead now reads “Master Craftsman” does not mean he has gone in for lamplighted research into his twig-furniture antecedents. He eats lunch at Burger King and volunteers that he "didn’t even finish second grade.” The main-street hut he works in, with a new refrigerator in the bedroom and a new litter of kittens in the bathroom, is a candidate for remodeling or oblivion in a local campaign to beautify Gunt-ersville.</br></br>Back in the 1930’s, Mr. Hand’s father, Ruben Jefferson Hand, cut down swamp willow off creek banks for his “hobo furniture,” which he bartered for food. “It was a way of making something without spending anything,” says Mr. Hand, since landowners were only too glad to get rid of their willow. The senior Hand, whose ledger will go on display alongside his son’s love seats when the Birmingham Museum’s Alabama Room opens late this summer, led a wayfaring De- pression life typical of the poor in one of the hardest-hit areas in the nation. “I don’t believe in welfare,” says Mr. Hand, who had to forgo school for work on farms and in sawmills.</br></br>Now Mr. Hand and other craftsmen are being reclaimed as "the soul of the state,” says Joey Brackner, Alabama’s official folklorist. "More and more states are seeing their craftsmen as resources,” he says. A few years ago the Alabama Tourism Bureau bought some Hand pieces for its welcome centers on the Tennessee and Georgia state lines. "Lord, we have given his name out to so many people it’s unreal,” says Pat Ship-pey, manager of the welcome center on Interstate 59.

text: Your New Year’s Day editorial “Don’t Just Bow to Mr. Nakasone” seriously underestimates the problem of United States competitiveness in the world economy.
