The decline predated both the current deficit and the rise in the value of the dollar. These have only made it more precipitous. And the challengers are not just Japan but South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Hong Kong as well. These four smaller countries export more to the United States than all of Europe.</br></br>The East Asians have succeeded despite their lack of natural resources by adopting national strategies to mobi-„ lize and shape their productive capabilities for economic growth and global competitiveness. Trade policy is a part, but only a part, of these strategies. More important, they emphasize work, savings and Investment to build a higher standard of living through increased productivity, rising real Incomes and acceleration of the shift of industrial structures toward activities that promise above-average growth and,technological innovation.</br></br>Furthermore, they assure lower costs of capital to their global competitors with government playing the role of a coach or quarterback, not that of a referee intent on blowing the whistle when rules are violated, or, worse, that of an adversary.</br></br>By contrast, the United States strategy, implicit as it may be, assumes the competitiveness of our economy and emphasizes increased domestic consumption, borrowing and distribution of income. text: WAS the economic recovery of 1983-84 the result of the Reagan Administration’s, supply-side policies or of the Keynesian stimulus resulting from big budget deficits?</br></br>Wallace C. Peterson and Paul S. Estenson of the University of Nebraska contend that, despite its supply-side rhetoric, the substantive economic policies of the Reagan Administration became Keynesian following the deep recession of 1981-82, which threatened Mr. Reagan with outright failure on the economic front.</br></br>Writing in the summer issue of the Journal of Post-Keynesian Economics, the Nebraska economists maintain that “substantative Reaganomics," by cutting taxes and sharply increasing Government spending, "took advantage of a simple but empirically valid principle, namely, that Government deficits stimulate economic activity.” Tax cuts and climbing military outlays, they say, led first to increased consumption and then to an investment surge. That concept is used by economists as a measure of what the budget deficit would be if the economy were operating at a standardized level of output and employment or unemployment. As now used by the Commerce Department, the standardized level of unemployment is set at 6 percent of the labor force. A bigger high-employment deficit implies greater fiscal stimulus; a lower deficit or surplus implies less stimulus or greater restraint.

text: THERE is a mystique to home ownership in American culture, but in the 1970’s the mystique was bruised. Traditional values in home-buying have reasserted themselves, they say, and the expectation of short-term appreciation is not as significant as it was.</br></br>But the tax benefits and leveraging characteristics of real-estate investment still tempt the investment-oriented buyer. Few other investments enable the buyer to borrow at least 75 percent of the purchase price, thereby opening the door to leveraged gains upon resale if the property appreciates in value. In those markets that are not suffering the aftereffects of an overheated market — among them New England and Long Island — investment-oriented buying appears to be fairly strong.</br></br>Moreover, the rise of for-sale primary housing in the condominium or homeowner-association form has created a promising avenue for investment ownership because the problem of maintaining the unit is minimized. Who cares about Arthur Crew Inman? During the 1920's he published several volumes of forgettable verse. If the excerpts he quotes In his diary are any Indication. His only other career, besides a brief spell of dabbling in the stock market with his father’s money, was to write down dally for more than 40 years every twist and turn of his experience, every tremor of consciousness. By the time of his death — he shot himself in 1963 after decades of wishing he had the courage to commit suicide — his diary ran to some 17 million words contained In 155 volumes.</br></br>It turns out that there are good reasons to contend with this book. The distillation of Inman's sprawling opus by Daniel Aaron, a professor of English at Harvard University, shows Inman to be an exemplary sufferer, a man who traumatlcally crossed the border from a past era into our own times. He was launched suddenly from Victorian sexual repression Into the freewheeling sex of the 20th century. Growing up In a well-to-do household with servants in an orderly Southern city, he ended up an underground man in a Northern city, which he experienced as chaotic and rapidly growing; hiding from its dazzle and commotion, he clung for security to a grotesque parody of an upper-class life. He traveled this distance in spasms of pain, about which he complained continually. He manipulated people at every turn to gratify his appetites, although he was not without moments of generosity. Ridden with symptoms, Inman indulged himself furiously, yet saw himself as a perennial victim — of his well-meaning parents, his upbringing and his culture. He is not an attractive figure, but he is an oddly captivating one.</br></br>And in Mr. Aaron’s adroitly edited version, Inman’s diary is a fascinating document, by turns bizarre and illuminating, poignant and obscene. It is an epic record of obsessive preoccupations and flamboyant pathologies — an idiosyncratic sexual life graphically depicted and of multitudinous aches and pains, physical, psychological and spiritual. When he is not scrutinizing himself, Inman draws shrewd, incisive portraits of everyone around him and then elaborates them with the most intimate, often malicious revelations.</br></br>The cast of characters — flappers and con artists, truck drivers and chorus girls. Southern cotton brokers and Northern lawyers, college students and matrons, adulterous osteopaths and evil-eyed psychiatrists, actresses and prizefighters — is worthy of a German Expressionist painting. Above all, there are women of every age and type, in costume and in various states of undress. Right-wing political speeches, wildly racist, frequently heating up to the point of tantrum, burst forth amid all the personal material. And as if to calm himself, Inman sets down just about everything that happened in American social, political, economic and cultural history from the end of World War I to the early 60's.

text: This chart shows the difference between the value of the S SP 500 futures contract and the corresponding value of the S.& P. 500 index itself The futures contract price derives from the S.& P 500 index plus a premium. That premium mainly reflects the fact that the future is bought on a small down payment and does not tie up the buyer's capital. This concept of the premium is called the "fair value'' portion of the futures contract. In practice, however, the premium continually fluctuates, and when the actual value exceeds or falls below the "fair value.'' there are arbitrage trading opportunities. This can cause abrupt price fluctuations in the equity markets, especially on days when stock trading is slow.</br></br>One day early this month in the midst of an otherwise lazy summer afternoon the stock market was grabbed by an undertow that pulled the Dow Jones industrial average down 21.73 points. The term refers to programs of orders from institutional investors and other professional traders to buy or sell shares in 100 or more large companies that are a surrogate for the broader Standard & Poor’s index of 500 stocks.</br></br>Such programs are often initiated by arbitrage opportunities when the current value of stocks reflected by the S.&P. 500 and the price of a stock index future on that index are out of line. An index future is a contract between two parties that allows an investor to bet on the general direction of the market over a short period of time.</br></br>The abrupt moves set off by the arbitrage play, market professionals say, stem from events unrelated to the prospects for the individual stocks that comprise the Dow industrial average and the S.&P. 500. text: CAMBRIDGE, Mass. — There are no short-run solutions to the economic problems that are affecting the relations between Japan and the United States. Both countries seem to agree that two-thirds of the enormous American trade deficit is caused by the overvalued dollar. But the remainder of the deficit still represents $15 billion, and this chronic imbalance is likely to grow larger in the future.</br></br>Focusing our energies on the export of beef, oranges, plywood or Haagen-Dazs ice cream will not help; neither will Prime Minister Yasuhiro Naka-sone’s urgings that every Japanese buy $100 of imported goods.</br></br>Instead we should think of our competitive position in the year 2000 and beyond. In thinking about that problem — especially the part unrelated to the exchange rate— several issues deserve clarification.</br></br>0 The net effect of Japanese economic practice since the 1950’s has been systematically to deny the profits of innovation to foreigners — and this affects Americans most of all. An American innovation is kept out or restricted by various formal and informal means until a Japanese manufacturer achieves international cost and quality levels. At that point the Japanese market is likely to open, but once a local manufacturer is well established, foreign entry is nearly impossible. In addition, the foreign innovator will soon have to contend with the “boomerang effect”: Japanese export of the very same product.</br></br>1 The profits of innovation are especially important to American companies. Our future lies in high technology, in which we still lead the world — though our lead is narrowing. As the innovation cycle shortens, so does the duration of this profit stream. But it remains a vital source of nourishment for the innovative enterprise, enabling it to develop, with some hope of success, the next generation of new and better products.

text: A HALLMARK of the Reagan Administration’s economic policies is to boost economic growth and productivity by dramatically increasing investment. So far, the hoped-for investment boom has yet to materialize. But even if it should come about, it will not bring the desired results. According to virtually every empirical study of the factors that are crucial to economic growth, the real priority should be to boost the quality of investment, not just the quantity.</br></br>Imagine, for example, that it is 1785 in the United States. Our capital stock includes such things as wooden plows, draft animals, hand pumps and Franklin stoves. Now perform a mental experiment on this economy: Assume that the rate of capital accumulation quadruples — but that innovative activity stops permanently. There would be some improvement in material well-being, but nowhere nearwhat actually happened.</br></br>Now try a mental experiment from real life—Germany and Japan at the end of World War II. Their capital stock was about comparable to that of many underdeveloped countries. But 20 years after the war ended these countries had achieved levels of pros- perity that far exceeded their prewar levels. The inherent advantage of Germany and Japan was the “knowledge base” embodied in their people; this proved to be more decisive than a capital base.</br></br>The first mental experiment assumed increased capital investment without innovation; the result was quite disappointing. The second assumed a skilled labor force and knowledge of advanced techniques — but a negligible capital base; here the result was quite heartening. Once again, the results suggest that the quality of investment is more important than the quantity. Output will grow slowly if we just add more plows and adding machines; it will grow substantially when we replace them with tractors and computers.</br></br>In “Modem Economic Growth,” Simon Kuznets, the late Nobel laureate economist, concluded that the “direct contribution of man-hours and capital accumulation” accounted for perhaps one-tenth of the rate of economic growth — “and probably less.” The rest he attributed to improvements in quality. text: The market for Government obligations is entering a new phase after being under the pressure of Federal Reserve System anti-inflation sales for the last six months. The changed atmosphere, although not yet clearly definable, is suggestive of. a market steadiness— that is, price stability as distinct from price inflexibility—for both the longest-term and shortest-term Treasury obligations for the foreseeable future.</br></br>The market’s new mood, visible since last Tuesday, is linked by the financial district to the implications of the Korean war, along with possible other factors. For the moment, anyway, there has been a cessation of central bank sales of the Treasury’s longest-term bonds at declining prices.</br></br>More distinctly discernible is a concurrent stabilization in the short-term part of the market. The pattern of bids now underlying all Treasury obligations maturing in fourteen months or less seems to indicate the maintenance indefinitely of the current 1^4 per cent borrowing rata for the Treasury's shortest-term interest-bearing oo-ligations. The new issue of 1% per cent notes which will mature on Aug. 1, 1951, was quoted all week on the premium yield basis of 1.24 per cent bid, 1.22 per cent asked.</br></br>The statistical net result of Federal Reserve operations in the market from June 21 to June 28 was a commentary in itself. During this week, which covered the subscription period to the Treasury’s new 1% per cent note issue, the central banking system’s holdings of Government obligations increased $538,500,000, the largest weekly increase since Septemher of last year. Holdings of bonds were reduced by only $6,000,000, the smallest weekly reduction since January.</br></br>felt, as before, by the Victory 2%s, callable in 1967. Other non-bank bonds were bid up progressively and closed the week at their best prices. On the other hand, bonds eligible for bank investment seemed unsure of their market status from here on in, especially the partly tax-exempt issues, whose market status is affected peculiarly by the proposed reconstitution of the corporate income tax on a 21 per cent normal, 20 per cent surtax basis. It would be imprudent, however, to view the market’s ‘‘new look” as anything more than a espot phenomenon marking a respite from a protracted period of central bank restraint whose tenure and extent have kept the investment .world, guessing for months. In fact, the financial implications of any new “defense effort" are, if anything, only a threat of more inflation—the very Federal Reserve sanction for “selling the market down.”

text: Installment lending by Federal Reserve member banks of this district now amounts to two-fifths of such credit in the country as a whole, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York reported yesterday.</br></br>Commercial banks, it pointed out, have steadily penetrated the field since the early 1930’s to become the largest source of such loans. _</br></br>In the current issue of its Monthly Review, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York pointed out that in this district member bank installment loans to individuals have increased approximately 760 per cent, from the war-depressed low of $95,000,000 in June, 1944, to $813,000,000 at the end of last year. The growth of such loans in these banks, it was noted, has been paralleled by that in member banks in the country as a whole.</br></br>At the end of 1949, it was pointed out, the largest single component of consumer installment loans was $235,000,000 of retail installment paper other than for automobiles. And this, the bank observed, contrasts with the situation in the remainder of the country, where the largest segment of member banks' installment loans consists of automobile paper. Personal installment cash loans, at $219,000,000, were the next largest component in this district, while repair and modernization loans amounted to $186,000,000, and automobile loans had the smallest total, $162,000,000.</br></br>“The greatest percentage increase during the 1946-49 period, however, occurred in automobile paper,” the bank commented. “This increase was bolstered by the especially large gains in the holdings of a few New York City banks, which have charged relatively low rates on personal loans.

J., Dec. 14—A program to curb inflation in the wake of expanding defense expenditures was recommended today by 220 economists representing twenty-seven of the nation’s colleges and universities.</br></br>Designed to constitute “the first line of defense against inflation,” the program calls for elimination of all unnecessary Government expenditures, raising tax revenues faster than defense spending grows to create a cash surplus, find more stringent credit restrictions.</br></br>The statement, drafted by a group of Princeton University economists, was circulated for signatures and released today by Prof. Richard A. Lester of Princeton.</br></br>The signers include Joseph S. Davis of Stanford and I. Leo Sharfman of Michigan; • both former presidents of the American Economic Association; Seymour E. Harris of Harvard, Edward S. Mason, dean of the Graduate School of Public Administration at Harvard; Arthur R. Upgre?n of Minnesota, Ray B. Westerfield of Yale and Clair Wilcox of Swarthmore.</br></br>The undersigned economists believe that prevention of inflation in the situation created by the expanding defense program requires as the principal line of defense, a substantial increase in taxation, reductions in expenditures at all governmental levels wherever this can be done without impairing national defense or other essential public services, and a more restrictive credit policy. The ba-sio cause of inflation, an excess of money demand relative to available goods, must be attacked. Only adequate fiscal and monetary measures can remove this basic cause.

text: The sources of inflation are too numerous and varied to permit a single or "painless" process of correction, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York declares in its annual report, issued today. The problem is not insoluble, however, the bank observes, adding that the challenge to public policy is to find and accept those techniques of control which will be effective during a period of rearmament that may last for years.</br></br>Signed by Allan Sproul, president, the report points out that 1950 presented a paradoxical record of economic change. The national economy, up to the middle of the year, had given a striking demonstration of the recuperative power and capacity for growth ‘‘of an enterprise system largely free of detailed Government intrusion.”</br></br>But by the end of the year, the report continues, the United States found itself—partly because of its success in maintaining a high-consumption economy at virtual full employment—"applying strict controls in order to make room for what was as yet a very moderate expansion in military production.” "Some of those who were strongly urging imposition of direct controls during the last half of 1950 did not recognize the essential interdependence between such measures and general fiscal and credit controls,” the report • observes.</br></br>“This was wishful thinking. Although there was no need of despair of bringing the inflation under control, its sources were too many and too varied to permit reliance upon a single corrective, or to expect the process of correction to be wholly painless.” Limitations on immediate expansion of production last year were the characteristic bottlenecks of full employment, principally a shortage of manpower in the labor force, and. a scarcity of certain critical materials,</br></br>"And the extensive rearrangement of productive capacity and manpower inevitable in the present transition period may be expected temporarily to interfere with the needed growth in productivity,” the report continues.

It has been pointed out that the strictest system the legislators could devise would raise only $10,-000,000 more revenue, which would fail to meet needs in the 1950-51 fiscal year by $125,000,000. Placing thousands of evaders on the tax rolls is a matter involving education as well as enforcement, and it cannot be done overnight It will take years. Just under $2,000,000,000 of United States money has been poured into the Philippines in the last six years. Only a small part of it was in grants, very little in loans. Most of it was in payment by military and other Government agencies for services. text: WASHINGTON, Jan, 16—The Federal Reserve Board increased the margin requirements in stock purchases and short sales today from 50 to 75 per cent in a move I calculated to head off undue credit [expansion in the securities field.</br></br>The board is also considering a renewal of its request to. text: Money in circulation throughout the nation passed the $30,000,000,-000 mark last week for the first time in history. For the week ending today, the situation is reversed, there being only five selling days against six last year. !Thus, while store sales showed a gain in the first of these comparisons, they weer down sharply for the current one. Moreover, with shoppers beginning their Christmas buying usually after Thanksgiving, the late arrival of that holiday shortens the active pre-Christmas buying period. text: The unexpected collapse of steel wage negotiations and President Truman’s request for legislation enabling the Government to seize and operate the steel industry ruffled financial markets last week. text: THE HAGUE, The Netherlands, March 22—A United States productivity expert crossing Eastern Prance by automobile this week would have several perplexing matters on which to write memoranda to bis boss.</br></br>From Besancon, at the foot of the Jura mountains, to Sedan, classic gateway for invading German armies, it is about 350 miles. There are some factories all along the way, particularly as one moves down the valley of the Meuse, past the battlefields of Verdun, where the earth, to this day, is tortured and pockmarked from the shells of 1916, and on toward the Belgian frontier. But by and large this is farm country.</br></br>If the productivity expert had never been along this way before his memoranda would reflect great discouragement He might even feel like resigning on the ground that all the propaganda, education, demonstrations and technical help offered to the French to increase agricultural productivity was like so much passing hot air against the immemorial bulwarks of habit and prejudice by which the peasant fortifies himself against change.</br></br>This week, on a fair day for early spring, a reasonably alert [traveler counted just six tractors between Besancon and Sedan — about one for every sixty miles. Last year France produced about 16,000 tractors, more than one-third of which were exported, which suggests they stand up fairly well in competition on world markets as to price and quality.</br></br>Although it is the high season of spring plowing, not one of these six tractors was working a field. Each was being used to haul heavy loads of pungent fertilizer of local origin along the road. The plowing was being done by men with horses.

text: NEW YORK’S department stores with a gain of 3.5 per cent in June are holding close to the 4 per cent average for the Second Federal Reserve District. In the latest Federal Reserve summary for the Second District, which includes the New York metropolitan area and New York State, department store sales showed the greatest gain in New York'3 Nassau County, the scene of substantial real estate boom and the area to which thousands of former New York City residents have migrated. In May, for instance, net sales rose 15 per [cent in Nassau County, compared with 1 per cent in the district as a whole, and a loss of 3 per cent in New York City. text: Some of the selling enthusiasm disappeared from the stock market last week after another jolt of selling drove prices down to the lowest levels in several years. Investors enjoyed the respite, wondering whether it meant an end to the long decline in the market which has reached a point where it is having a depressing effect on the nation’s economy. Washington has become aware of its implications and has taken steps to reassure ‘ taxpayers on the future outlook.</br></br>Ending of the excess profits tax and a 10 per cent cut in individual income taxes will come through 'the first of the year as scheduled, according to George M. Humphrey, Secretary of the Treasury. While he is not pessimistic on the business outlook, he does expect some soft spots to develop in the coming months. It is his belief that if any readjustments are to be made, it would be best for the country if one industry at a time were involved and not all industries at the same time.</br></br>Of course, there is always a calming effect when one is told that his taxes will be cut. text: Relaxation of restrictive monetary policies by the Federal Reserve in the late spring now appears to have constituted the most important single development in the improved earnings position of large New York City banks.</br></br>Due to a “time lag,” only partial indication of the current bank prosperity will be provided by the third-quarter condition statements and interim earning reports to be published this week, but the outlines of the general improvement are I rapidly emerging.</br></br>Such benefits as the higher level of interest rates on loans and securities, stabilization of deposit totals and the midyear reduction of reserve requirements have yet to make their full impact on operating results. Moreover, with the expiration of the Excess Profits Tax Law in prospect, barring a prolonged recession, the earnings outlook was never more favorable.</br></br>According to M. A. Schapiro & Co., Inc., bank analysts, this year’s net operating earnings of tile seventeen large metropolitan banks after taxes, but before security transactions and transfers to reserves, are likely to be in excess of $170,000,000, a gain of 6.8 per cent over 1952. Such a total would represent a net return of 7 per cent on the banks’ aggregate capital funds of $2,500,000,000. Based on existing rates, dividend payments of $98,000,000, would mean a “payout” of 57 per cent against 60 per cent in 1952.</br></br>In the late spring the Federal Reserve Board acted to provide reserves to the banks by open market purchases of Treasury bills, and by cutting legal reserve requirements against deposits. Combined, these moves were intended to create a primary market for government securities, enabling the banks to participate in the Treasury’s essential financing of about $6,000,000,000 of tax anticipation certificates. text: To the Editor of The New York Times : The editorial in The New York Times of Nov. 9 on "Jobless Who Won’t Work" indicates that oi/ the basis of Government statistics "lazy" individuals draw'little or no unem- ! ployment compensation. Under the insurance laws of the several states, compensation is/not paid unless a worker.,has; Ipst his job through no fault of his' own, is willing to take another job, and is actually looking for one. Reports of his efforts to find work are also required—in some states every, week, in others every other week.”</br></br>It may be that figures don’t lie, but they appear to be grossly distorted if applicable to New York., There is nothing in the New York law1 which requires reports every week or every other week of the claimants’ efforts to find work.</br></br>. Many states, in addition, have in their law a period of disqualification for unemployment due to marital obligation, employers’ pension plans and dismissal .payments. Claimants can and do collect unemployment benefits and pension or dismissal payments at the same time. *</br></br>To be available in New York the claimant has to show that he is capable, ready, willing and able to work in his usual occupation or any other for which he is reasonably fitted. Although token efforts to obtain employment may not be sufficient to be eligible for benefit, a “lazy” individual may obtain benefits because he is not required actively to seek work for. each week he is applying for benefits.</br></br>A glib individual under existing New York law might easily convince a claims taker at the Unemployment Compensation Office that he is in the labor market when in fact all he wants is rocking-chair money. text: ALBANY, Feb. 1 —Governor Dewey’s hopes of balancing his 1954-55 budget are keyed to the continued high level of prosperity in the year just past and a conviction that no serious economic recession is in sight.</br></br>To cover the expenditures he plans for the fiscal year beginning April 1, the Governor expects revenues of $1,125,750,000, which is more than the state has ever collected in any year and $40,000,000 more than last year’s record.</br></br>Mr. Dewey, In his budget today, is relying principally on two of the State's biggest moneymakers—the personal income tax and the corporation franchise tax —to produce this extra revenue. He estimates that the first will be $14,650,000 greater next year and the second $10,000,000 larger.</br></br>In both cases he is on relatively solid ground. These taxes, although paid in 1954-55, are based on. income received in 1953-1954, a period during which business activity and employment in the state reached record levels.</br></br>Of the twenty-four taxes and revenue sources listed in the Governor’s budget, only four are expected to produce less money in the 1954-55 fiscal year than the present estimate of what they will bring in during the year now closing.

text: For the first time in two decades, the stock market is undergoing a detailed Federal study. The last inquiry, conducted in the gloomiest days of the depression, resulted in stringent laios to regulate security transactions. Now, with, stock prices at record levels, the Senate Banking Committee is trying to determine whether new Government action is called for. Here is ait A-B-C explanation, in the form of questions and answers, of some of the tilings the committee is looking into.</br></br>A.—Stocks represent shares of ownership In a specific enterprise. Some companies have only a few shares of stock; ot.hers have millions. General Motors, the country’s biggest manufacturing corporation, has 92,894,500 shares of common stock and 2,835,644 shares of preferred stock. The owners of a company's stock are the owners of the company. They are entitled to vote for its directors and in that way to exercise a voice, proportionate to their ownership, in the control of its affairs.</br></br>Shares earn money for their owners in the form of dividends. These represent the amount voted to stockholders by the company’s directors on the basis of its income, financial needs and prospects. In most cases preferred stock calls for a fixed dividend, usually at the rate of 4 or 5 per cent of the face value of the stock each year, and the holders of these securities must get their dividends before owners of common stock get anything.</br></br>dividend at all. How much profit a company makes is the primary factor in determining how much it will distribute in dividends. Most companies try, however, to maintain a steady rate of dividends. In good years, extra dividends may be declared. In bad years, dividends may be cut or eliminated.</br></br>A.—Generally, when people speak of the stock market, they think in terms of trading on the New York Stock Exchange. Eighty-five per cent, in dollar value, of all securities bought or sold in organized exchanges are traded on its floor. Listed on the "Big Board" are the shares of 1,200 companies, with more than 10,000,000 employes. These companies produce 90 per cent of the nation’s steel and oil, handle 95 per cent of its rail and air travel, make 70 per cent of its automobiles and trucks, and generate 75 per cent of its privately produced power. The market value of their stock is $170,000,000,000 at current prices. In addition to the New York Stock Exchange, there are a score of smaller market places for the transfer of stock. The largest of these is the American Stock Exchange, formerly the Curb Exchange, in this city. Many stocks are not listed on any exchange. They are traded directly in what are known as “over-the-counter" sales.

text: The two most important financial news stories last week appeared . within forty-eight hours of each other, and the central figure in each was the stock market. This was the announcement by the directors of General Motors that the corporation planned to raise $325,000,- 000 in the next few weeks through an issue of common stock. Present stockholders, the company directors revealed, will be given subscription rights to the issue, which will be underwritten by a nation-wide group</br></br>If there is one theme on which nearly everyone is in agreement it is that there is far more emphasis than there should be on interest-bearing capital in the financing of American industry as contrasted with equity capital. (This is a matter not of poor managerial judgment, hut of built-in obstacles to equity financing, stemming chiefly from the favored position enjoyed by interest-bearing securities under our tax laws.)</br></br>It is perhaps almost as widely agreed that if we are to have an expanding industry, with a strong foundation of equity capital, then we must be prepared to provide a wide public market for equity securities.</br></br>It is probably safe to say that a majority of persons would be prepared to go further on this point. Security loans, they would say, are a necessary part of such a market. text: Whether or not a Ford strike is averted, it is clear that the contract negotiations between the company and the United Automobile Workers have added a new dimension to collective bargaining. Agreement has been reached on the principle that an employer has an obligation to provide financial protection for jobless workers beyond the limits of state unemployment insurance systems.</br></br>This does not mean the “guaranteed annual wage" the union first demanded. But there is little reason to doubt that the principle accepted by Ford will spread through most mass-production industries. Union pressure wall be strong for its adoption In the rest of the automotive field, in electrical manufacturing, in steel, in rubber, in railroads, in shipping and in many other sections of the economy. With pension and welfare programs already broadly established as responsibilities of industry, employers will now add another layer of security to that provided by government.</br></br>The economic implications of this trend cannot be assessed in absolute terms. Certainly it is desirable to give industry a greater stimulus toward stabilizing employment by leveling out the ups and downs of production that mean overtime work one month and layoffs the next. Certainly it is constructive to provide increased purchasing power for workers idle through no fault of their own, especially when our state legislatures have been so slow to bring unemployment insurance checks up to reasonably adequate levels in most states.</br></br>It is a demonstration of the vitality of the democratic process that so fundamental a change in old concepts of labor-management relations was made by voluntary agreement without government intervention. Union and company representatives worked out their own accord on principle and on the amount of money that should be used to implement the principle. Yesterday’s hectic down-to-the-wire talks were concerned primarily with how much security the proposed expenditure could buy.</br></br>But the whole move for industry-financed unemployment support systems will prove destructive if employers and unions forget that the price must be paid out of increased productivity. There are some industries in which any rise j in production costs is bound to aggravate deep-rooted economic woes, i Coal mining and textiles are two areas in which automatic extension of the notion that what Ford does \ all industry must do, would jeopardize the solvency of the employers j and the marketability of their prod- ' vet Even within prosperous indus-1 tries there will be many companies that cannot assume new costs with- | out ifiviting bankruptcy.

text: The last Wall Street investigation prior to the recent “friendly-study” of the-stock market by Senator Fulbright’s Committee on Banking and Currency was not, as many persons believe, the Pecora inquiry of 1933-34. It was the so-called anti-monopoly investigation conducted by the Temporary National Economic Committee half a decade after I that.</br></br>i Far and away the biggest offensive mounted by the committee on that occasion was an I elaborate effort to show that a I handful of banking firms in New York’s financial district had for years held a tight monopolistic grip on the nation’s security underwriting business.</br></br>That inquiry—sometimes referred to,' with the Pujo hearings of 1912 in mind, as the Second Money Trust Investigation— was destined to have a strangely unhappy epilogue a decade and a half later. It was revived on Oct. 30, 1947, in the form of an anti-trust suit in the New York District Court. Judge Harold R. Medina listened for more than two and a half years to the presentation of the Government’s case, then threw it out of court without even calling upon the defendants for a rebuttal.</br></br>Many will recall that inquiry, however, for a less epic and more beguiling distinction. They will remember it as the only Congressional inquiry in which the authors employed, the professional services of an expert in semantics. This tutor, selected, presumably, because he had just produced a popular work on that subject, provided for the committee’s guidance a short vocabulary in which words and phrases were evaluated not for preciseness of meaning, but in terms of their emotional content.</br></br>Many will recall, no doubt, the author’s observations, for example, on possible references to "Government spending.” "Spending," he warned >the committee, “is a ‘bad’ word. Avoid it like a copperhead!” If a situation should arise in which its employment was unavoidable, then, he counseled, it should be “firmly associated with ’sales,’ ’wages,’ ‘purchasing power,’ or other ‘good’ words, tenderly regarded on the folkways.’’ study of the stock market might make history by turning out pretty much as its author intended it should when he first proposed it, back in January. The hearings were certainly not unduly inquisitorial (some may wonder, indeed, whether they were inquisitorial enough). If they strayed into fields that at times seemed only very tenously related to the question at hand this was ascribable, by and large, not to. any tendency on the part of the committee, or its chairman to transform the hearings into a fishing expedition, but to the witnesses themselves. Some of the latter, at least, while by no means reluctant to give the committee the full benefit of their opinions, appeared to find £he subject that they had'come to Washington to discuss either too specific or too confining for their talents.

text: WASHINGTON, Feb. 28-Mention “resort to the printing press” and the man who abhors inflation (and who doesn’t?) shudders. But, at the moment, the notably anti-inflationary United States Treasury is asking Congress for renewal of the Government’s only direct authority to do just that.</br></br>Yet, even though this is the sort of thing that watered such foreign currencies as the French franc, there appears little reason for loss of sleep among the brotherhood of anti-inflationists. The Treasury has no intention of using .the authority except for very brief periods and for largely technical reasons.</br></br>The authority in question is what one student has called the “quicksand of currencies”—the right of a government to borrow directly from the central bank. In this case, it is the right of the Treasury to borrow from the Federal Reserve System.</br></br>Where does the Federal Reserve get the money ? It creates the money, right out of thin air. It doesn’t actually use a printing press, but it creates checking money, which is the same thing.</br></br>at the twelve Federal Reserve Banks are arbitrarily increased by the amount of the borrowing, and the Federal Reserve Banks get what amount to promissory notes in return. There is suddenly more money available for use in the country than there was before, with no more goods to spend it on. That is the very essence of inflation.

text: WASHINGTON, Nov. 17 — Probably the single most important domestic goal of the Eisenhower Administration is to prove that a modem economy can have full employment over an extended period without inflation.</br></br>The evidence of the Administration’s first four years is not conclusive. The next year or two very well could be. The Administration’s economists have genuine hope that the goal can be achieved.</br></br>Consumer prices, the so-called "cost of living," have risen about 2.2 per cent this year to a record high after three years of stability.</br></br>They began rising in April and have gone up in every month since, except August. The last figure was for September—117.1 on the Federal consumers’ price index, which uses average prices of 1947-49 as 100.</br></br>Wholesale prices rose sharply beginning about the middle of last year until they reached a peak in September, 1956—a little over 4 per cent above the average for all of 1955. Since then, however, they have steadied and even declined a little. They have shown no exuberance for over a month.

text: WASHINGTON, May 2—The staff of the Federal Reserve Board concluded in a study made public today that “there is real question” whether there can "soon” be another surge of automobile buying on credit like that of 1955. text: In an editorial dealing with the stock market decline, appearing in this newspaper on Oct. 10, it was observed that “such a readjustment, however painful, was overdue.” The editorial went on to add: “It is not a healthy sign for the economy when corporate stock prices reach the point where they yield less to the holder than he can obtain from corporate bonds."</br></br>Two days after that The Times published a letter to the editor from a correspondent who "wondered” whether it wouldn’t be possible to improve the paper’s “timing” of such comments. “Couldn’t the Times,” the writer inquired, “deal with such aberrations at an earlier stage” ?</br></br>The short and obvious answer to this, of course, would be that The Times, in common with most responsible newspapers, probably didn’t regard it as part of its editorial function to pro-vide its readers with a stock market tipster service. Few editors in full possession of their senses, it is fair to say, would knowingly indulge in what the onetime chief editorial writer for The Wall Street Journal, William Peter Hamilton, once referred to as “the most gratui-! tous form of human folly” —namely, attempting to call the turn on the stock market.</br></br>A few days ago A. Wilfred May of The Commercial and Financial Chronicle, in an address delivered before a price forecasting seminar of the Econometric Institute, took the occasion to recall a classic observation on this subject by the late Lord Keynes. Said Keynes: “Professional investment may be likened to those newspaper competitions in which the competitors have to pick out the six prettiest faces from 100 photographs; the prize being awarded to the competitor whose choice most nearly corresponds to the average preferences of the competitors as a whole. Each competitor has to pick,</br></br>not those faces which he himself finds prettiest but those which he thinks are likely to catch the fancy of the other competitors, all of whom are looking at the problem from the same point of view.” Not even the Federal Reserve Board, which has the power to restrain speculative activity through the raising and lowering of mandatory mimimum margins, would think of intervening in the market on the basis of its own arbitrary decision that stocks were priced too high. It had not exercised these powers in the more than two years between its last margin rise, in April, 1955, and the recent downturn in stock prices. It has refrained from doing so, and quite correctly, despite the fact that stock prices advanced roughly 80 points, as measured by The Times average, since the first of its two most recent margin increases, in January, 1955.

text: SAN FRANCISCO, Aug. 9— On the eve of his eighty-third birthday anniversary, Herbert Hoover sighted two clouds over the country today. I don’t know. I can make no useful comment. You listen to Mr. [Nikita S.] Khrushchev [First Secretary of the Soviet Communist Party] one day, and the next day to somebody else.” ON BIRTHDAY EVE: Former President Herbert Hoover posing yesterday .atop the Mark Hopkins Hotel in San Francisco. text: A year ago this month the Government released statistics confirming what many had suspected •—that the 1957-58 recession was the worst since World War II. text: The recession is having an adverse psychological effect on retail business. It manifests itself by a wave of over-cautiousness that tends to paralyze the thinking of some merchandisers. text: LONDON, Jan. 21—The Government raised the bank] rate today from 4 per cent to 5 per cent. The increase in the rate, the key to most interest rates, startled Britain’s ! Because there have been signs of inflationary pressures in Britain’s booming economy, many economic experts had considered a rise inevitable, but most had not expected it so soon. An increase of a full 1 per cent was more than many thought likely.</br></br>The Bank of England’s bank rate is analogous to the United States Federal Reserve System’s discount rate. This is the rate paid by the system's banks on money borrowed from, it In both cases an increase discourages banks from borrowing and as a result reduces their lending.</br></br>Move Is Precautionary Both the Treasury and the Bank of England emphasized after the announcement that the move was precautionary and that there was nothing fundamentally wrong with the British economy.</br></br>Some business men minimized the effect of the change. But the National Union of Manufacturers said that internally its .effect could be only bad. It [will mean higher retail prices [in the long run and will hurt the smaller concerns, which normally borrow to finance development, the organization said. Morgan Phillips, secretary of the Labor party, saw the move as evidence that the economic situation was “not nearly as rosy” as the Government contended at the time of last fall’s general election and since then.</br></br>As evidence that the economy is sound, the authorities note that Britain's exports were about 5 per cent higher last year than in 1958 and that the | country earned a substantial surplus in its dealings with the rest of the world. For months Britain also has maintained a remarkable degree of price stability despite the boom in business and industry.

text: Judging by the performance] of the stock market last week, Wall Street is a good deal less] concerned about the near-term and long-range state of the economy than Washington is.</br></br>Even as President Kennedy said that he saw no definite indication of an upturn from the present recession, the stock market advanced on a tremendous wave of trading. Volume topped the 5,000,000-share mark during four of the five trading sessions and prices, on average, reached the highest level since last June. The advance, however, was not one sustained drive. It came in fits and starts and for a good part of the week the market was most aptly described as “churning.”</br></br>On Tuesday, for instance, volume on the New York Stock Exchange soared to 5,800,000 shares, the heaviest turnover in five and a half years, or since former President Eisenhower’s heart attack in September, 1955. Yet on Tuesday, The New York Times combined average of fifty representative stocks managed to show a net gain of only 0.77 ipoint. The average closed on Friday at 377.69, for a gain during the week of 6.27 points. This brought the gain for the year 'to date to 32.55 points. Trading was the heaviest since the week ended July 22, 1933.</br></br>There were various explanations for the remarkable activity in the market, but worry about a further deterioration in business conditions was certainly not one. Rather, it appeared a matter of the return of the specter of inflation—never far away, to be sure. Many investors apparently were convinced that the Kennedy Administration's various legislative proposals and other programs would touch off a new upward price spiral. Some were selling for that reason; some were buying for the same reason. The twain met in the market and the result was the heavy turnover.</br></br>It was considered significant by some analysts that investors were showing revived interest in steel and motor shares, representing two of the weakest segments of the economy. text: President Kennedy was asked at his news conference last week whether he had purposely avoided using the word “recession” in a speech the previous day about the national economy. President Kennedy took office convinced that the nation was in a slump, and he.set out immediately to apply restoratives. He has ordered a variety of stimulants on his own authority and has bombarded Congress with requests for the kind that require legislation.</br></br>But so far Congress has adopted none of the President’s proposals and in most cases has not even begun action on them. text: IN the course of its examination of the U. S. monetary and credit system, the Commission has studied the rote of the Federal Reserve System and the effectiveness of its control measures. It has examined the debt management and monetary activities of the Treasury, as well as the broader aspects of its fiscal policy.</br></br>The Commission also examined the lending activities of the Federal credit agencies, the regulatory policies of the Federal and State governments, and their effect upon the dominant part of our financial system, the private sector. It has examined the problems of government organization and administration of monetary, credit, and fiscal policies. It has examined certain problems of international liquidity and credit and the balance of payments adjustment mechanism.</br></br>From these examinations several recommendations for structural and institutional changes have emerged. For the most part, these recommendations propose either structural and institutional changes that will contribute to the more effective functioning of the economy or propose broad guides for specific policy decisions. The Commission has tried to avoid specific policy prescriptions for particular problems. It has tried to confine its recommendations and suggestions for change only to situations fchere the present structure has not worked well.</br></br>It has avoided recommendations for change merely for the sake of change or merely to achieve a more logically consistent structure. The recommendations do not call for the wholesale overhaul of our financial structure. They consist of many small changes which frequently affect revolving trends.</br></br>The recommendations are based on the fundamental assumption that the economy will continue to be largely a private enterprise economy. This form of economic organization, with its stimulus to individual initiative, has been a key element in explaining our outstanding record of economic growth and national well being and is well suited to perform effectively in the years ahead. The Commission believes, however, that both private enterprise and government have major and complementary roles to play in achieving national objectives, and that neither one nor the other can do the whole job. Consequently, the recommendations deal with both government and private enterprise, and they try to strengthen the effectiveness of both.

text: THE Commission in its deliberations has dealt with fiscal policy only in its most general sense. Thus it has examined the effects of changes in the budget surplus or deficit on economic activity. The role of fiscal policy in economic stabilisation is faT better understood today than it was during the depression of the thirties, and it is now likely that the adjustments m fiscal policy undertaken in major inflations or depressions will be appropriate in direction if not in magnitude. The challenge for the future is to improve the use of fiscal tools to smooth lesser fluctuations of prices, output, and employment, and to promote economic growth.</br></br>The federal budget has served as a useful stabilizing'force in the economy, partly through the exertion of automatic changes in tax receipts and transfer payments as incomes rise and fall, and partly through deliberate changes in tax and spending programs. The combination of automatic and discretionary budget forces has generated surpluses in prosperity and deficits in recession. The surpluses helped restrain booms and the deficits helped cushion the recession and aid recovery. But neither the size nor the timing of fiscal policy have been appropriate to the movement of the business cycle.</br></br>output result in automatic changes in tax yields and in certain outlays by the government. As national income falls, for example, the yield of the personal income tax falls also, while payments for unemployment compensation rise. Consequently the absolute decline in income available for spending is less than the absolute decline in national income. As national income rises the opposite effect takes place. Tax receipts rise and unemployment compensation payments drop. These cushioning effects happen automatically without administrative or legislative interference. Hence they are known as automatic stabilizers.</br></br>It i9 impassible to estimate precisely the effectiveness of existing automatic stabilizers. The best available evidence indicates that during the postwar period the built-in flexibility of the federal budget offset between one-third and two-fifths of the fall (or increase) in the gross national product. This is a sizable fraction, far greater than that prevailing before World War II. Recent experience with recurrent and moderately severe recessions raises the question whether the automatic stabilizers can and should be strengthened to play a greater role in reducing the amplitude of cyclical fluctuations.</br></br>stabilizers without altering the existing level of tax rates and government expenditures, has considered these possibilities: (1) Changes in the tax structure. text: If the stock market decline is a “riddle wrapped in a mystery inside an enigma,” then today’s unsure bond market must be a “myth wrapped in a clichS inside a complexity."</br></br>Bond men thus garbled facetiously last week the diction of Winston Churchill and President Kennedy as they pondered why high-grade bonds did not keep rising in price in orthodox accompaniment to the 1962 stock market’s major secondary slide.</br></br>In capitalist folklore, the bond market should go up when the stock market goes down. Forces that make for rising stock prices —business expansion and big borrowing from the banks and the public—tend to use up the money supply. The intensified bidding for debt capital causes the prices of bonds to rise.</br></br>On the other hand, forces that cause stock prices to go down— a decline in business activity and a donline in borrowing from the banks and the public—generally tend to malke bond prices rise, because surplus investment funds are forced to compete for the purchase of a dwindling supply of bond issues.</br></br>True, the sharp stock sell-off of May 28 was accompanied, by the dumping of bonds, but this was viewed as only a momentary affair, dictated by the need of investment houses and individual investors to improve cash liquidity in the wake of the drastic overnight shrinkage in equity values. .

text: By ARTHUR KROCK WASHINGTON, May 4—The fiscal philosophy of the Kennedy Administration—that the best method of reducing unemployment and increasing the gross national product is a simultaneous combination of tax cuts and more Federal spending—was already mixed up when Secretary of the Treasury Dillon addressed the Chamber of Commerce here this week. By the end of his speech this fiscal philosophy was whirling even faster in the mixer.</br></br>In January, the Secretary had stigmatized as “unrealistic” the arguments of many economists and industrialists that the need for a tax cut was not. as the President and .he were insisting, to avert a for another combination to start the economy on a steady march toward higher levels. This proposed dual program was a tax cut, in company with reduced Federal spending which would reduce the prospective deficit for fiscal '64.</br></br>In May, when Dillon spoke to the Chamber, the first of these arguments had already been sustained by the facts. Not only was there no recession, but economic conditions had improved on their own, since Congress meanwhile has done nothing about cutting taxes. But, even though Dillon—by holding out the hope that new revenues created by the economic improvement would, despite a concurrent tax cut, permit the reduction of the prospective '64 deficit from $12 to $11 billions— conceded "reality” to this proof of a forecast he had found "unrealistic” four months previously, he continued to find "unrealism” in the argument that there should be a simultaneous slash in Federal spending.</br></br>(2) The danger is not fanciful because "President Kennedy was very close to launching . . . this new mythology when, in speaking April 19 ... to the American Society of Newspaper Editors in Washington, he asserted that 'a cut of $5,000,000,000 now from the proposed Federal budget... would cause 1,000,000 fewer jobs’ ” by the end of fiscal '64.</br></br>(3) In supporting his estimate, Mr. Kennedy "assigned a great part of the responsibility for the 1957-58 recession to what he described as the “tremendous drop in 1957 of Federal purchases, in the defense area particularly, and credited it with having added to the miseries caused by what he apparently believes to have been a generally mistaken fiscal and monetary policy—namely a $12,-500,000 deficit in 1959, the largest outflow in a period of years of gold and dollars amounting to nearly $12,000,000,000, and a recession in 1960.”

text: CIVIL rights, the war in Vietnam, inflation and taxes— these are minor problems compared to one which millions of American parents are now facing, that of helping their children learn the “new mathematics." The problem isn't made any easier by the fact that the stores are currently displaying a dozen paperback books about mathematics whose covers suggest, somewhat misleadingly, that they will provide first aid to the perplexed. As a matter of fact, only six of the books are of value to parents, and these only with qualifications.</br></br>Before assessing their individual merits, it would be well to consider just what the new mathematics is and why it was introduced into school curricula.</br></br>For many years there had been rather general agreement that the teaching of mathematics was unsuccessful. The standard explanation of this failure is that the traditional curriculum taught only what was known before 1700 while from that date to 1955 mathematics had changed as much as had physics, chemistry and biology. (The implication is that students knew of these purported changes and refused to take an interest in the antiquated material.) At any rate, early in the 1950's a number of mathematicians and teachers decided that the curriculum was at fault and had to be refashioned.</br></br>Beginning in 1952, one new curriculum was fashioned by the University of Illinois Committee on School Mathematics. In 1954 the Commission on Mathematics of the College Entrance Examination Board started a campaign for adoption of the new mathematics. After 1957, assisted with grants from foundations and governmental agencies whose purses seem to have been loosened by the advent of Sputnik, a dozen other projects, dominated by college professors, produced their versions of new curricula. Of these projects the most influential is the School Mathematics Study Group, established by the American Mathematical Society, the organization of mathematicians concerned with research. The new curricula were at first directed toward the reform of high-school mathematics courses but soon afterward were extended to include the elementary Schools.</br></br>One could challenge the conclusion that the failure of mathematics education in the past was due to the poor cur- riculum. One may have doubts —as I do—about the panacea qualities of the new math. Nevertheless, it is now a fact of American educational life, and for better or for worse, a legal precondition of parenthood; many a modem parent must face the prospect of helping his children cope with it, for help they do need.

text: The surging wave of anti-Americanism in South Vietnam is reflected in the slogans scribbled on a Saigon wall. The Vietnamese words say “Down with the Thieu regime.” The English words refer to Ellsworth Bunker, United States Ambassador.</br></br>SAIGON—If there are any truly hopeful or complacent Americans still left in the huge United States mission here, last week should have made it more difficult than ever for them to believe that they are loved, even liked, or occasionally appreciated by the South Vietnamese. For the politicians, the university students, the angry Buddhists, the adolescents who hate the war and refuse to be pulled into it, the working class man who blames inflation on the foreigners, are all trying in different ways to tell him how they feel.</br></br>Anti-Americanism in South Vietnam is most particularly seen and sensed in Saigon, but only because peasants in the countryside have fewer chances to express it. Since 1965, when the buildup of United States military forces began, few Americans here thought it would all be rosy between the two races. But fewer still thought the day would come when a warning would be issued by the United States Embassy for staff members not to travel alone in Saigon because of recent acts of violence against Americans. Last month, Vietnamese students here pulled an American M.P. from a jeep, beat him, and burned the vehicle.</br></br>After the embassy warning— in which employes were advised to travel in pairs—officials were embarrassed by the attention it drew to a problem they, naturally, would wish to conceal. An embassy spokesman said last week the warning was actually more of a precaution than the result of specific anti-American attacks (on which no figures, of course, were available) but it was too late to convince anyone.</br></br>The warning makes sense. The mood of the Vietnamese in Saigon has been increasingly ugly since last May. There are fewer Americans in Vietnam — in Saigon, too—but those that are here are hated more. It is unsafe, even stupid, for a foreign woman to walk alone after 9 P.M. even in the heart of downtown Saigon. Boys riding in pairs on Honda motorcycles will try to snatch her handbag. The same boys will also try, and nearly always succeed, in cutting camera straps on the shoulders of Americans, and even pulling off wristwatches from the arms of men. Theft is not the only reason: What happens in Saigon is not quite the same small mean crime that happens so often in New York. Here, it is a way of getting back, of showing the Americans that the Vietnamese can threaten them, too.

text: By M. J. KOSSANT Is it or isn’t it ? Business forecasters pondering whether the economy is in a recession have been unable to reach a consensus. Forecasters should know by now what kind of ’pattern will prevail for the rest of 1967. After all, the results of the first two months are already in and it should not be overly difficult to figure out what happens next.</br></br>But forecasters appear to be in agreement only in observing that the economy is experiencing a definite slowdown in business activity. They are at odds over whether this current pause will be followed by a fresh upsurge or a further decline.</br></br>This dispute over the outlook is renewed proof that business forecasting remains an imprecise art rather than a precise science. It also emphasizes the special difficulty in determining economic turning points— those critical periods when activity undergoes decisive change.</br></br>But whether or not the economy is at a turning point now, most forecasters are sufficiently disturbed by what has been happening to business activity to question the need for tax increases called for by the Johnson Administration, Even those who believe the slowdown will soon come to an end do not think that the ensuing rise will be vigorous enough to warrant curbing demand through an increased tax on individual and corporate incomes.</br></br>In taking this position, forecasters are not only suggesting that it is a mistake to formulate economic policy too far in advance of actual developments, they also are saying that the whole idea of managing the economy through the “fine tuning" of monetary and fiscal instruments is unlikely to work during the most critical periods if forecasters cannot decide with assurance whether a turning point is at hand.

text: 'T'HE productivity of Martha Graham remains joyfully unabated—works continue to pour from her. During her current season at the George Abbott Theater she is offering no fewer than three' major new creations, which will bring her total for three seasons to seven, a record that few leading choreographers could match.</br></br>The first of her three new works was given on Saturday night. Called "A Time of Snow,” it is based on the love story of Heloise and Abelard. This story of love in a cold landscape of despair, of passion won and hope lost, of chill and lonely fidelity, lends itself easily to the mood of reflective retrospection that .Graham has made peculiarly her own.</br></br>So many of her works spiral around a heroine caught in the still center of the tragic whirlpool, looking up . and backward at the vortex of her life. Graham has given so much to the dance in the physical terms of pure invention and imagination— almost every modem-dance performance in the world is to some extent a celebration of her genius—that it is easy to miss her special gift to the dramatic theater, which is the abandonment of linear time in favor of free-structured development “A Time of Snow” is typical of this freedom taken of time. It opens with Heloise looking back on her solitary life in the convent, after she has been parted from her lover, Peter Abelard. Then she recalls the youthful days of her love, when the world was quick and green and she was what Abelard once called a “windflower.” Then, with no break of continuity, the body of the dead Abelard is brought to her. Love has run full circle, and all that remains' are the flowers of memory, the blossoms of legend, so that even today lovers bring flowers to their graves in a Paris cemetery.</br></br>.1 suspect, be less than apparent to someone who had no'prior knowledge of it, and indeed a reading of the work’s program note is prob- ‘ ably essential to even its cursory appreciation. But no one has ever passed legislation against reading program notes. The story of these 12th-century lovers is perhaps less familiar than the poetic associations of their names. Peter Abelard was a great scholar, and one of the founders of the Sorbonne in Paris. He was master of the Cathedral of Notre Dame when its canon, Fulbert, asked him to be tutor to his 17-year-old niece, Heloise. Abelard, by then a middle-aged man who had never had. a mistress, fell hopelessly in love with the young Heloise. They became lovers, but were parted by Heloise’s vengeful father, who put .thugs on Abelard to castratehim.</br></br>Years passed — with Abelard in a monastery and Heloise in a convent. But their love endured, all through the long, snowy winter of a remembered spring. When Abelard died, his body was brought to Heloise. Legend has it that when she, in turn, was buried beside her lost lover at the Pdre Lach&ise Cemetery in Paris, his arms opened out to receive her. It is this legend of lovers that Graham has taken.

text: When economists talk about how inflation erodes the value of the dollar, it may be difficult for the average person to grasp the meaning. text: VIENTIANE, Laos — The gold trade of Laos—which once accounted for more than a third of the Royal Lao Government's tax income — is well into its second year of recession. The decline of gold tax revenues has put pressure on various American-backed financial assistance programs to Laos, but probably for the best. It has also forced Laotian planners to look elsewhere for funds, increase some taxes and tighten up its tax collection procedures.</br></br>The import of gold, which Laos alone among Asian countries permits with no restriction, once provided the national treasury with an income of somewhat less than $500,000 a month. In a country where the national budget — including a 50 per cent United States subsidy — annually hovers around $32-million, and per capita income — never ac- curately measured — as probably lass than $100 a year, the gold trade, like foreign aid, was one of those gifts from heaven that allowed a backward country with virtually no tax here to muddle through financially.</br></br>During the best years of the gold trade — from mid-1966 until the beginning of 1968 — sometimes as much as eight tons of gold a month would enter Laos, on which the Government imposed an 8.5 per cent duty. In contrast, during last May, only 1,850 kilograms of gold entered Laos and the month before that 1,325 kilograms.</br></br>be smuggled into nearby countries to Indian millionaires, Thai businessmen, Cambodians who wanted to place their future in something more reliable than non-convertible riels. American pilots and Embassy officials also bought gold jewelry, which could be brought into the United States. An identification bracelet weighing as much as 10 ounces of pure gold still is a common sou-venlor of Laos. But the main market for Laotian gold was South Vietnam where the massive American build-up was providing much easy money, but little financial security. Vietnamese returning to Saigon on flights from Vientiane would carry kilograms of the stuff, often concealed in garments and luggage.</br></br>In January, 1968, just before the Tet offensive, 6,704 kilograms of gold entered Laos through official checkpoints — a good but not exceptional tally. Presumably a similar amount left the country, though Laotian officials do not record gold exports. During February, 1968, less than half that amount was imported. Although local businessmen and officials predicted a resurgence once the Vietnam fighting slackened, by July, 1968, the trade had declined to a low of only 925 kilograms. Despite an occasional good month since] then, the volume of trade has never again resumed its old level. Financial advisers to the Laotian Government say the decline has continued chiefly because of instability in the European gold market and a crackdown on gold smuggling into South Vietnam.

text: Labor Day finds many union leaders wondering whether it is time to put a treadmill in place of the collective bargaining table. text: CHICAGO, July 17—Dick Martin, a 32-year-old construction worker, is one of a small number of American hourly wage earners whose incomes have kept them ahead of inflation in the last year or so. But he finds little consolation in that.</br></br>He and other journeyman plumbers in Chicago won an increase of 70 cents an hour last June 1, a rise of 11 per cent over last year. This brought Mr. Martin $28 a week more, increasing his gross pay to $210.</br></br>But Mr. Martin and other construction workers here seem to be singularly unimpressed that Government statistics show they are better off in their struggle to outpace rising prices than any other blue-collar workers in the country. Anyway, they say, their gain over inflation is so small that it has gone unnoticed.</br></br>“If the figures show we’re ahead, then I guess we are,” said 6-foot-5-inch Mr. Martin, scraping the roof of a crowded construction trailer near the site of the new International Business Machines building. “But I don’t believe that it’s made any difference in the way my family and I Jive. text: Ebullient Herman Kahn, who boasts that under all those 300 pounds of friendly fat there lies a lean and sinewy intellect, is Prime Minister Eisaku Sato’s favorite futurologist. Mr. Sato freely confesses to Tokyo visitors that he and his party have benefited mightily from Mr. Kahn's confident predictions — “surprise-free,” he calls them—that by 1990 Japan will probably pass the United States in per-capita income, and that by 2000 she will probably equal her partner across the Pacific in gross national product.</br></br>As a nation, the Japanese seem to be one of the world’s worst worriers, constantly preoccupied with putting their best foot forward. Yukio Mish-ima commits suicide in the stem Samurai tradition, his dagger making a deep, straight cut across his abdomen, his teeth firmly gripping his tongue—and thousands of staid, golfplaying Japanese businessmen, diplomats and journalists cringe in all the world’s capitals. (What can their Western bridge partners and golf mates be thinking of them now? What unfathomable depths do they see lurking beneath the all-too-ready Japanese smile?) Along comes Dr.</br></br>Kahn, with his deep-throated chuckle and his cheerful bedside manners, telling his Japanese patient not to be poor-mouthing all the time, that he is in much better health than he thought, that the rise of his country ranks with the agricultural-industrial revolution and the post-industrial revolution as one of the three most important processes in human history.</br></br>“Thanks to Herman Kahn,” Japanese writer and politician Shintaro Ishihara says, “even barbers are talking about the G.N.P.” “The Emerging Japanese Superstate” presents the background reasons for Mr. Kahn’s optimism: the arguments he has worked out over the depths of the Japanese character. Some readers may consider his predictions too glib, or exclaim that the</br></br>G.N.P. is not all there is to a nation’s soul. (Mr. Kahn, incidentally, would agree.) It is nevertheless, a jolting and provocative book.

text: Philadelphia’s public schools started the season with a $30-million budget deficit. That meant the elimination of some 600 teaching positions, a good chance that the school year would have to be cut by four weeks—and an end to all extra-curricular activities. That last turned out to be the unkindest cut of all.</br></br>Parents, students, civic groups and both mayoral candidates demanded the immediate return of the high school football program. To the rescue: Democratic mayoralty candidate Frank Rizzo, who prevailed upon Philadelphia Eagles' owner Leonard Tose to donate the $79,000 required to save football.</br></br>The school board agreed to take the money, and even to restore all extra-curricular activities—if Mr. Rizzo would promise that, should he be elected, he would provide the board with sufficient extra funds to forestall the four-week cutback in the school year. And Mr. Rizzo said he’d go along with that—provided the school board would first permit him a post-election audit of its books.</br></br>So it was that Philadelphia had its first school football practice session last Tuesday —and education officials nursed a spark of hope about •their budgetary woes. Still, School Superintendent Mark R. Shedd had his doubts: "We are operating on the political promises of two candidates, and that’s a lot of fluff. I want to see the color of cash."</br></br>The drive was sparked by Mrs. Ben Ruhlin of Cuyahoga, Ohio, and her 30-member committee. The object: passage of a constitutional amendment that would overturn two 1963 Supreme Court decisions and,permit prayers in public schools. In opposition was Representative Emanuel Celler, dean of the House of Representatives and chairman of the Judiciary Committee, who refused even to clear the proposal for a floor vote. And he had lots of company last week as Protestant and Jewish groups sent 38 leaders to Washington to register . their opposition. Among the points they raised: No one has ever been able to come up with a definition of nondenominational that everyone could agree on.

text: The drive of the Nixon Administration to swing the United States’ balance of payments from deficit to surplus is running into a serious obstacle—rising unemployment in Europe and Japan. There is danger today that</br></br>the non-Communist world, which since the end of World War II has been led by the United States, may split into isolated and protectionist blocs. text: WASHINGTON—Prior to Aug. 15, 1971, the Administration’s economic policy was one of benign neglect. At home, unemployment was allowed to increase and growth to stagnate in the misguided belief that this would cure inflation. Instead, it produced both 6 per cent unemployment and 6 per cent inflation.</br></br>Abroad, the policy was to consider the dollar invincible. .Foreign central banks would continue to accept endless dollar deficits, no matter how badly over-valued the dollar was. No fundamental realignment of currencies,</br></br>But then came Aug. 15 and the New Economic Policy which the President has encumbered with obeisances to the false gods of trickle-down at home and protectionism abroad.</br></br>At home, the price-wage freeze was accompanied by a tax-reduction program which has now been substantially enacted by the Congress. In essence, the tax program gives corporations and their stockholders an $S-billion a year annual tax reduction mainly through the 7 per cent investment tax credit and rapid depreciation. After the first year, the tax (1) By obviously discriminating against the wage earner, it destroys the social contract upon which effective wage-price controls must be founded. Labor’s increasing unwillingness to go along with meaningful wage restraints is due in large measure to the inequality of sacrifice brought about by the tax bill.</br></br>(2) The nation’s "fiscal dividend,” out of which was to be paid the cost of health and education and environmental control and revenue-sharing in the decade of the seventies, has been effectively wiped out by the permanent fracturing of the revenues implicit in the tax-reduction bill.
