text: WASHINGTON — How much do you know about one of the most widely watched statistics in the United States — the official monthly estimate of national unemployment?</br></br>Following are five simple, yet not-so-simple, statements about unemployment. Mark them -true or false and score yourself. A perfect score qualifies you as assistant commissioner of labor statistics. Three correct qualifies you to head a Presidential commission on unemployment statistics.</br></br>1. False. A sizable increase in employment will often result in lower unemployment, but higher employment can also be accompanied by no change or even a rise in unemployment. Not infrequently, the labor force will increase more than employment — because of new entrants attracted by improved job opportunities, population growth, statistical variability or other reasons — so unemployment will also rise. Sometimes unemployment will fail to respond to even a sharp rise in jobs. In April 1983, for example, a sizable, 350,000 rise in total employment (seasonally adjusted) failed to significantly reduce unemployment because of a rise in labor force participation.</br></br>2. False. Unemployment is not involuntary for everyone. Doubtless the higher short-term unemployment that occurs in recessions is largely Involuntary. But what is voluntary is not easy to define and measure objectively. One definition of “voluntary” unemployment Includes any unemployed person who will not accept a job unless it pays a higher wage than that person last received.</br></br>3. False. The official unemployment rate is an incomplete measure of the available supply of workers. The official count — not unreasonably — includes only those people who are actively seeking work. There are millions of others outside the measured labor force — members of an inactive labor reserve — who are either available for work under existing labor market conditions or who would be available if conditions were better. Some are discouraged workers, many with only modest wage demands, who are not looking for jobs because they think none are available. Many more non participants would be available for work only at above prevailing wages — some at excessive or inflationary wages such as might occur in a very tight labor market. 4. False. Lower unemployment rates are not always better. Certainly It is beneficial all around to reduce recession-level unemployment, such as we are still experiencing. But as cyclical joblessness declines and as the more intransigent structural components of unemployment are encountered, short-term inflationary pressure begin to build. At some point in a tightening labor market the gains from additional jobs and economic growth diminish relative to the economic costs of rising inflation.

text: The inflation of modem job titles has advanced so far that “vice president” is beyond rescue. But if vigilant citizens will bestir themselves, it may not be too late to protect “president.” “Vice president” was lost without a shot. Even in Washington, where the office is often ridiculed (“not worth a pitcher of warm spit”), at least there is only one of them, and he does what he’s supposed to do: prepare to act vice, in the place of, the President. But there’s probably no other organization with only one vice president, or where a vice president truly serves as No. 2.</br></br>On the contrary. Vice presidents have proliferated faster them co-editors-in-chief of high school yearbooks. To be a vice president now is to have about as much pomp, prestige and power as a first lieutenant.</br></br>A friend in a large advertising agency reports that its 1,100 employees include 150 ordinary vice presidents. The next step up is senior vice president. There are 11 of those. Then one reaches executive vice president, a once-exalted rank that used to mean No. 2. The agency has 11 of those. Likewise, in a large New York bank, one becomes a vice president after about five years. There are hundreds of them, plus 50 senior vice presidents, plus 10 executive vice presidents.</br></br>It’s no use railing against this vice-presidential inflation. It reflects organizational needs. A leader who designates a single successor risks seeing power flow to him. An organization may wish to reward several officers for achievement in different specialties. Or it may want customers to think of their sales representatives, if designated vice presidents, as senior corporate officers.</br></br>Underlying all those needs is a failure of language. Civilian organizations have developed all the tiers and complexity of the military but lack terms (captain, major, colonel) readily indicating who’s higher in the hierarchy. So when “vice president” becomes a catch-all, that puts pressure on the next job up — which is exactly what’s happening at Chemical Bank.

After years of regulatory setbacks and operating problems — and of living with a drastically reduced market share in its basic stock options business — the C.B.O.E. wants to tailor its services to a financial community where the traditional distinction between securities and commodities trading is becoming increasingly blurred.</br></br>With that in mind, the C.B.O.E. is also negotiating the purchase of the New Orleans Commodity Exchange. There have been other moves. Last fall the C.B.O.E. began trading its first option on a debt security, Treasury bonds, though this has met with poor response. And it expects to soon offer options on Ginnie Maes.</br></br>In addition, after several failures, it is trying once again to bridge the generation gap between itself and its estranged parent, the Chicago Board of Trade, hoping the two exchanges can cooperate on joint trading ventures.

text: WITH the rise in the Consumer Price Index by four-tenths of 1 percent last month, making an increase of 4.2 percent over the preceding 12 months, the Government has announced how much taxpayers will save on their 1985 income taxes to adjust for inflation. Starting Jan. 1, income tax brackets, the zero bracket limit, the standard deduction and personal exemptions will all be raised 4.1 percent.</br></br>As welcome as the start of indexation will be for individual taxpayers, whether it means a net saving or only an offset to the statutory rise in Social Security taxes, it means a loss of revenues to the Federal Government in the face of widening budget deficits. How big the revenue losses from indexation will be depends on future inflation and the economy’s rate of growth.</br></br>In making its long-term budget projections, the Congressional Budget Office assumed that the Consumer Price Index would rise 3.9 percent in 1984 and thereafter would average 4.8 percent annually from 1985 through 1989. And the agency assumed that real economic growth would average 3.2 percent between 1985 and 1989.</br></br>On those assumptions, indexing would cost the Treasury $5.7 billion in the fiscal year 1985, with the revenue losses mounting to $30.9 billion in 1987 and $64.7 billion in 1989.</br></br>Since the rate of inflation on which the Government will now base indexation during 1985 has been announced as 4.2 percent, rather than the 3.9 percent assumed by the C.B.O., the revenue loss in the current fiscal year, which began Oct. 1, will be closer to $6 billion.

text: Economists on Wall Street never seem to be at a loss to explain the latest wiggle in interest rates, although they concede that nobody has perfected a way for accurately predicting rates.</br></br>This week credit market participants are waiting anxiously for the Federal Reserve Board chairman, Paul A. text: SHOULD the Federal Reserve regulate margins in the market for futures and options on financial instruments and stock indexes? Or should this power remain with the individual exchange? text: WASHINGTON — It should have been one of Ronald Reagan’s best weeks. The stock market closed at new highs amid spreading euphoria that economic recovery had begun at last. On Capitol Hill, the bipartisan Social Security rescue package easily cleared its first tests, and it appeared that a nasty confrontation over jobs and aid for hard-pressed families would be avoided.</br></br>But like radio interference, outside events kept intruding on Mr. Reagan’s message that America was “on the mend” and that his Administration was in command.</br></br>The White House’s attempt to contain the crisis at the Environmental Protection Agency, for instance, was plainly failing. Despite Mr. Reagan’s newly declared support for Anne McGill Burford, the beleaguered agency head, Administration officials were privately speculating that Mrs. Burford would have to resign. Allegations of mismanagement, and of political manipulation and favoritism in the program to clean up toxic wastes, grew. Mr. Reagan also abruptly found himself dealing publicly with the military situation in El Salvador. Just before leaving for the West Coast to attend a series of rain-soaked ceremonies with Queen Elizabeth II, the President hastily summoned Congressional leaders to the White House to say that he would soon be asking for a sizable military aid package to prevent a leftist overthrow of the Central American government.</br></br>“You see, this is all part of a plan,” said one White House official, his voice dripping with sarcasm. “We fig- ured the news on the economy and on Social Security was just too good. We had to figure some way to keep it off the front page.” Indeed, Mr. Reagan’s frustrations flashed in Los Angeles, where he accused the television networks in particular of focusing on “bad news” because “good news isn’t good for the ratings.” The comment was a fresh illustration of the extent to which governing boils down to a battle for the nation’s attention span.</br></br>In some respects, Mr. Reagan had only himself to blame for his failure to get credit for his recent successes in Congress. Precisely because the White House thought it would be counterproductive, Mr. Reagan has lately avoided ringing speeches on matters there. The White House reasons that Democratic support for the $165 billion Social Security package can be counted only if Mr. Reagan refrains from boasting that his leadership carried the day. And he has avoided comment on the $4.9 billion plan voted by the House to create jobs and feed families in hard-pressed regions, though he has quietly signaled that he could approve most of its features. Here, the President’s strategy was clearly to try to ward off a major jobs bill later by embracing a minor jobs bill now, and to lower the decibel level until economic recovery strengthens his hand.
label: yes
metadata__headline: Static Breaks In on Reagan's Good News

text: RIO DE JANEIRO, March 2 — Rio de Janeiro's legendary carnival is a more serious affair than usual this year. It is taking place during Brazil’s worst economic crisis in decades, with both the sacrifice of buying the glittering “fantasy” costumes and the need for release from the hardship of daily routine greater than ever.</br></br>It is also the city’s first carnival under a Socialist Governor, Leonel Brizola. Already criticized for rising crime rates and deteriorating public services, Mr. Brizola has made a bid for popularity by spending $20 million on permanent viewing stands — quickly christened the Sambadrome — along the route of the samba parades. But his many political foes seem no less eager to find a way of blaming him for the “failure” of carnival.</br></br>Hence, behind the pre-Lenten explosion of carefree hedonism that ends on Ash Wednesday, March 7 this year, less frivolous economic, political and cultural issues are at stake. Fortunes will be made or lost amid the dancing, drinking and sexual exchanges, and the political good will enjoyed by the local government will either increase or erode in the coming days.</br></br>Mr. Brizola seems fully aware of this. He personally became involved in organizing carnival, and his Deputy Governor, Darcy Ribeiro, spent months insuring that the Sambadrome was finished on time, appeasing samba clubs upset by unexpected changes in the program and justifying the huge investment by a state government that says it is almost bankrupt.</br></br>“In previous years it cost half as much to build tbe temporary stands, so the Sambadrome will be paid for in two years,” Mr. Ribeiro said in an interview. “Dining the rest of the year, the part under the bleachers will accommodate 200 classrooms for 16,000 students. The area will be used for dances and concerts every weekend. It will have the city’s first carnival museum. It’s going to be one of Rio’s tourist attractions.”

text: People in the 1980’s play art the way they play horses. They also play art the way they play the stock market, at no matter what level. Art in recent years has been judged by whether or not it “performs.” As a hedge against inflation, the paintings of J. M. W. Turner have “performed” in spectacular style, whereas the pound sterling has not. As a repository for hot money, moreover, art beats real estate, beats the stock market and beats the gold bar.</br></br>This is neither a distinguished nor even a reputable attitude, but it is widespread. It is the basis of almost every dinner conversation that turns to the subject of art. Every newsstand has magazines that cater to it, and they can’t all be losing money .</br></br>Besides, art is prestigious. Even today, it stands for exalted achievement. Just as you are what you eat, so you are what you have on your wall. To own a late van Gogh may not put you up there with van Gogh in the scale of human achievement, but it links your name with his. No longer are you simply Judson Jinks. You are the owner of the Judson Jinks van Gogh, and the beneficiary thereby of a satisfaction on which no price can be set. You don’t have to stick to established values, either. If a 25-year-old painter called Christopher Cannibal is the talk of every table in town, what greater bliss than to hear it said that “Jinks was in there early with Cannibal”?</br></br>But how to get in there early with Cannibal? Thirty years ago there were just two or three galleries to go to. Today you have to begin on Madison Avenue above 79th Street. From there you work the terrain, fanning out to left and to right, all the way down to 57th Street. On 57th Street you are in heavy territory, both to the east and the west. Chelsea cannot be ignored. SoHo and Tribeca have to be covered in depth. Nor should the area around Tompkins Park, in the East Village, be left out.</br></br>There’s just no knowing where Cannibal, the new young man of the hour, may surface. There may be a uniformed security man at the door, and the walls may be covered with best quality brown velvet. You may have to endure the ordeal by elevator that is a speciality of 57th Street. Elsewhere, white marble may surround the work of Cannibal, and the view may extend over 16 square miles. But Cannibal may also be found in a broken-down den to which no former function may decently be assigned. It is the prerogative of Cannibal to be everywhere and nowhere.

The standard economic view is that unrestricted competition provides lower prices, higher quality and better services for consumers. The greater the number of sellers competing for the favor of the individual buyer, it is believed, the more that buyer will benefit.</br></br>But the presumed advantages of unrestricted competition can be realized only if the resources needed by sellers are essentially limitless. Those who deregulated trucking and airlines, for example, correctly assumed that new firms could easily assemble the equipment and personnel they needed to enter the businesses. The deregulators accurately predicted that, as competition multiplied, at least some consumers would find real bargains among the many new choices available to them. This pattern holds true for shoes, refrigerators, computers and many other industries as well; banking is a major exception.</br></br>For bankers, the basic resource is money itself, and the supply of money is by no means limitless. It is regulated by central banks, in our case by the Federal Reserve Board. Some critics believe that the Fed is too restrictive, others argue that it is not restrictive enough, and some accuse it of inconsistency. Either way, it still regulates the money supply. text: WASHINGTON — A little more than a year ago there began an experiment in relations between Congress and the Federal Reserve Board— an experiment with both potential benefits and potential dangers.</br></br>It resulted from a joint resolution of both houses of Congress whose main requirement was that the Federal Reserve report every three months, alternatively to the House and Senate Banking Committees, on its targets for growth of the money supply over the coming 12 months.</br></br>Arthur F. Burns, the Federal Reserve chairman, at first was wary of the new procedure, but now he says, in the name of the entire board, that he "welcomes” it and has found it useful. It has produced. among other things, the first publicly announced Federal Reserve targets for monetary policy.</br></br>But the potential dangers remain. The chief one all along has been that Congress—made up, after all, of politicians — might try to force the Federal Reserve into a monetary policy more expansionary, and hence possibly inflationary than the central bank thought desirable.</br></br>The first milestone was a report by the Senate Banking Committee based on the latest testimony from Dr. Burns who appeared in early May. The committee gave the Fed high marks for its performance during the recovery phase of the economy last year and early this year, but it raised the possibility of a serious clash in the future.

Y.</br></br>In 1973, when he was first elected mayor, Ed Hanna promised to turn Utica, a sooty and disheveled city on the Mohawk River, into "a wonderful and beautiful place to live.” Considering the condition it was in, this would have required something on the order of a miracle. When the knitting mills moved South in the 1930's, jobs became so scarce that nearly 20 percent of Utica's population eventually left town. The rate of unemployment among the 90,000 who stayed was the second highest in the state, with 10 percent of the work force chronically unemployed. Along Genesee Street, the city's main drag, storefronts displayed practically as many “For Rent” signs as ads for merchandise. The one hotel had closed its doors, and outside of a few patrons at the lone movie house and several couples hanging around Critic’s Lounge waiting for a 350-pound stripper called “Elephant Woman," at night the central city was almost deserted.</br></br>Utica did have one of the first urban renewal projects in the country—a 1950's plan to tear down some old buildings and erect a modern office, shopping mall and hotel complex. But after two decades of squabbling and mismanagement, the city had nothing to show for it but a seven-acre mud-hole and parking lot in the middle of its central business district. As for political leadership, the city government had traditionally been a jungle of cronyism and petty graft.</br></br>When Utica took to cutting down its dying elms, for instance, the Parks Department listed many of them in its records as “Republican” or “Democrat," according to whose house they stood in front of. text: WASHINGTON — When a bill to provide $4 billion In public works jobs came to the Senate floor recently as part of the new Administration's stimulus plan, there was little disagreement about the total but a great deal of disagreement about how to distribute it among the states. Ultimately, although the purpose of the bill was to relieve areas with severe unemployment, in order to muster a majority of Senators the statistical definition of "severe” had to be relaxed so that more states would qualify for funds, and each state had to be guaranteed a minimum allocation of $30 million whether it needed it or not.</br></br>The incident was a classic example of the wonderland of Federal grant-in-aid formulas,, in which ostensible national objectives—such as fighting poverty, educating children, or promoting mass transit—become blurred in the attempt to gain legislative support for the funding necessary to achieve them. Rather than disinterestedly deciding who are the poorest, the hungriest or the most in need of mass transit funds, a member of Congress tends to vote for the distribution formulas that benefit his own constitutents the most. The struggle over these formulas pits section against section, and urban legislators against rural.</br></br>_In the end, the formula is determined by what is necessary to produce a successful coalition. Senator Abraham Ribicoff, Democrat of Connecticut, described the process during the debate on the jobs bill. The Senator said, “Day in and day out on this floor all of us get these sheets of paper [with various proposed formulas], and everybody fiddles around with a formula to find out . . . whether it will give a dollar more to 26 states, and then you become a winner—and then the national interest is forgotten.” More often than not, the losers in recent years have been the states of the highly urbanized industrial Northeast.</br></br>give a rural bias to the Federal formulas and channeled a disproportionate amount of aid into the southeastern states, said Sally W. Swartzmiller, an economist in the New York State Budget Division. “But to make doubly sure that the funds for material and child health, crippled children’s services and child welfare services went into rural areas, the number of rural children and the number of rural live births were counted twice for part of the distribution.” Similarly, Federal aid to education is based on the number of children between the ages of 5 and 17 in families with incomes below the poverty level, currently $5,780 for a family of four. Welfare payments are counted as income. In New York City, many hard-pressed families are above the national poverty level, partly because the welfare payments, reflecting the cost of living, are higher in the Northeast than in other sections of the country.</br></br>The original revenue sharing bill, in 1972, also illustrated how formula factors can produce disparities among regions. The bill provided more aid Tor areas without plumbing facilities and with a large number of persons per room. Northern Senators pointed out that most buildings without adequate plumbing were in the South, and that lack of heat was a more appropriate index of poor living conditions in the North. Overcrowding, they said, is also far more prevalent in the South than in the North, where a family of four in the Bronx might live in a six room apartment, albeit unheated and rat-infested. As a result of these objections, plumbing was dropped from the formula, but overcrowding, defined as a housing unit with 1.01 persons or more per room, remains a factor that brings some places more aid. Similar compromises had to be accepted to obtain Federal aid for mass transit. To get the legislation through Congress, members from New York agreed to a formula that was based on population and density rather than on the number of riders. Consequently, New York City, with 31 percent of the nation’s mass transit riders, gets 14 percent of the funds.

text: The weekly reports on the nation's basic money supply fuel the growing struggle between Arthur F. The phenomenon that it is supposed to measure cannot be measured accurately. The weekly re. ports that set Wall Street spinning are only estimates that may subsequently be revised, sometimes enough to alter the perception of the M-l’s behavior. The implications of its movements for the future of the economy are subject to sharply differing interpretations. Such considerations raise questions as to whether the M-l deserves all the attention it is receiving.</br></br>The M-l is but one of a number of monetary aggregates, M-2, M-3 and so forth, that purport to measure the deposits and currency owned by American families and business (other than banks). It is the narrowest of such aggregates, hence the name M-l, including only means of payments—that is, currency in circulation and checking deposits. The concept is thus a simple one.

text: WASHINGTON—From the staff of Congress and from the economists at the Brookings Institution have recently come sober assessments about inflation. It is, they say, a deeply entrenched force in the American economy, and, they maintain, the Carter Administration has not come up with an anti-inflation policy that is likely to make much of a difference.</br></br>"The outlook for inflation is not encouraging," Brookings, a liberal research organization, said earlier this month. "The deepest and longest recession since 1938 has not reduced the underlying inflation rate of 5-6 percent a year.. .. The general rate of inflation will not be greatly moderated by the policies proposed by the new Administration.” Few in government would disagree with that assessment of the underlying rate: The stubborn persistence of that rate is one reason Federal Reserve chairman Arthur F. Burns expressed concern about last week's slide in the dollar, provoked by the release of June’s record trade deficit figure. A weak dollar, Mr. Burns noted, generates inflation by increasing prices for imported goods.</br></br>Why is inflation so persistent? What is the Carter Administration doing to combat it, what is it not doing and why?</br></br>The answer to the first question sheds some light on the next two. Despite the existence of idle resources and labor, costs and prices defy the laws of economics and chase each other up. That is in large part because expectations of inflation tend to be self-fulfilling. As the Congressional Budget Office put it in its recent report: "During the last decade, inflation has become embedded strongly in our economic machinery. The rapid spread of cost-of-living-adjusted labor contracts, the reflection of inflationary expectations in a broad spectrum of interest rates and the automatic linking of major Federal entitlement programs to consumer price increases are a few important examples."</br></br>In 1976, Jimmy Carter gave indications that he would actively seek to break inflationary psychology. As a candidate from the South wooing the liberal northern wing of the Democratic party, Jimmy Carter said he was for stand-by wage-price controls; as President, he has proved to be anything as an activist on the wage-price front.

text: THE week’s economic and financial news seemed baffling, frustrating, even doublecrossing. The national economic indicators pointed up, but the stock market went down. The Commerce Department’s key index of leading indicators increased 0.4 percent in February, showing how early the economy began bouncing back from the severe winter freeze that had dropped the same index 1.2 percent in January.</br></br>The recovery was getting back into stride. Retail sales were up; factory orders were up; housing and construction contracts were up. Secretary of Commerce Juanita M. Kreps said she expected real gross national product in the first quarter to "hit just under 4 percent." Real G.N.P. in the January-March quarter had earlier been estimated to come in half a percentage point lower.</br></br>Mrs. Kreps and her economists might still be on the low side. Some private economists calculate that first-quarter G.N.P. may have climbed at an annual rate of about 4.5 percent. The April-June quarter, making up for the unusually rough winter, is likely to advance at an annual rate of 7 percent or more. The economy in the second half of 1977 promises to settle down to a 6 percent annual rate of gain.</br></br>Given the overhang of 7.3 percent unemployment— 7 million workers—and Mr. Carter’s commitment to get unemployment down, which was the main plank in his economic campaign platform, the President is not going to be talked out of his stimulus program by the conservatives’ argument that the economy is moving fast enough, or too fast, already. The jobless rate is still likely to be too high by the end of 1977, even with the fiscal stimulus.</br></br>Yet, where Washington sees itself as cautiously prodding along a fairly good but still inadequate recovery (inadequate to kick off capital spending or reduce joblessness fast enough), Wall Street fears the fiscal hypodermic needle. It fears worsening inflation and climbing interest rates—perceived as poison for the securities markets.

text: The Wall Street Journal observed unhappily the other day that its editors had begun to fear “that the control of this inflation exceeds not only our will but our intellect."</br></br>This dire sentiment was accompanied by a survey of economists that showed a general consensus that inflation would continue well into the Eighties; several believed, however, without much solid evidence, that the American economy will have righted itself by the end of the next decade.</br></br>If so, it certainly won’t be because nature and the market were left to go their ways unmolested. If nothing else, continuing American dependence on imported oil obtained at OPEC prices will require direct action of some kind. The very occasion of the Journal’s despondence was its concern whether Chairman Paul Volcker and the Federal Reserve Board have sufficient power to “manage the world supply of dollars in such a way as to produce an acceptable level of stability.” (And that was before the dollar tumbled to $500 an ounce against gold.)</br></br>At risk of appearing to assert superior “intellect” to that of The Wall Street Journal, which Milton Friedman himself might tremble to do, the following are some steps that appear to me to be worth serious consideration in the Eighties — by no means offered as a “strategy” to fight inflation but only as individual actions that might be useful within such a strategy: 1. Strong oil conservation measures. Hobart Rowen of The Washington Post has pointed out, for example, that a computer-based coupon gasoline rationing system costing about $2 billion to operate could reduce consumption by 1.5 million barrels a day. At prospective oil prices, that would save $14 billion a year. To save as much by pricing would require a $1.50 tax per gallon of gasoline, running up other prices ruinously.</br></br>2. Selected controls. As a stopgap to allow time for long-term measures to be developed, price controls on such necessities as food and medical care would be of great help to most Americans. text: Gregg Easterbrook argues that the financial crisis is just a small cloud over the road to rapid global innovation.</br></br>A MERICA could use a truly Whiggish book right about now. Acknowledging the stresses renewed change will bring, Easterbrook nevertheless believes that the pluses vastly outweigh the minuses. Easterbrook argues that globalization is indeed like a sonic boom: “noisy, superfast, covering huge amounts of territory." text: In the last decade or so, the American economy has been undone by a series of bubbles. First there was the dot-com boom, in which start-ups without business models were suddenly worth billions of dollars. Then after a brief recession, we began speculating about real estate, so that Las Vegas tract homes tripled in value before they even had roofs. The latest suspect for a bubble is gold, which has doubled in price over the past three years.</br></br>Why are bubbles such a persistent feature of financial history? Economists argue that these speculative frenzies are caused in part by market failures like too much liquidity or lax regulation. Cognitive psychologists, meanwhile, see bubbles as a case of pattern recognition gone awry, as people extrapolate the past into the future. In recent years, neuroscientists also have become interested in 'bubbles, if only because the financial manias seem to take advantage of deep-seated human flaws; the market fails only because the brain fails first. Read Montague, at Baylor College of Medicine, has spent the last few years trying to decipher the bits of brain behind our irrational exuberance. It’s microeconomics at its most microscopic.</br></br>Montague’s experiments go like this: A subject is given $100 and some basic information about the stock market. After choosing how much money to invest, the player watches as his investments either rise or fall in value. The game continues for 20 rounds, and the subject gets to keep the money. One interesting twist is that instead of using random simulations of the market, Montague relies on real data from past markets, so people unwittingly “play” the Dow of 1929, the S&P 500 of1987 and the Nasdaq of1999. While the subjcctsare making their investment decisions, Montague measures the activity of neurons in the brain.</br></br>At first, Montague’s data confirmed the obvious: our brains crave reward. He watched as a cluster of dopamine neurons acted like greedy information processors, firing rapidly as the subjects tried to maximize their profits during the early phases of the bubble. When share prices kept going up, these brain cells poured dopamine into the caudate nucleus, which increased the subjects’ excitement and led them to pour more money into the market. The bubble was building.</br></br>But then Montague discovered something strange. As the market continued to rise, these same neurons significantly reduced their rate of firing. “It’s as if the cells were getting anxious," Montague say s.

text: IF you were going to turn to omy one economist to understand the problems facing the economy, there is little doubt that the economist would be John Maynard Keynes. Although Keynes died more than a half-century ago, Ills diagnosis of recessions and depressions remains tile foundation of modern macroeconomics. Ills insights go a long way toward explaining the challenges we now confront.</br></br>According to Keynes, the root cause of economic downturns is insufficient aggregate demand. When the total demand for goods and services declines, businesses throughout the economy see their sales fall off. Lower sales induce firms to cut back production and to lay off worker^. Rising unemployment and declining profits further depress demand, lending to a feedback loop with a very unhappy ending.</br></br>The situation reverses, Keynesian theory says, only when some event or policy increases aggregate demand.</br></br>Tlte economy's output of goods and services is traditionally divided into four components: consumption, investment, net exports and government purchases. Any expansion in demand lias to come from one of these four. But in. each case, strong forces are working to keep spending down. consumption The Conference Board reports that consumer confidence is near its record low. It is easy to understand why consumers are so scared. House values have declined, 401(k) balances have shrunk and unemployment is up. For many people, the sense of economic uncertainty is greater than they’ve ever experienced. When it comes to discretionary purchases, like a new home, a car, or a washing machine, wait-and-see is the most rational course.</br></br>A bit more saving is not entirely unwelcome. text: Lisa Appignanesi reviews two centuries of volatility in the treatment of supposedly mentally ill women.</br></br>BACK when Zelda Fitzgerald, her skirts wet from diving into public fountains, was accelerating from madcap toward outright madness, a Wharton School economist named George Taylor made the seemingly fey observation that hemlines rose and fell with the stock market, proposing a caus- at connection between two presumably separate spheres of human enterprise. Fashion, as the now familiar “hemline index" suggested, is socially determined. With prosperity come optimism and tolerance for risk; women are emboldened to show off a more daring length of leg. But what of more empirical, utilitarian domains? Surely doctors hypothesize independently of whatever forces drive style. Take, for cxnmplc, the diagnosis and treatment of mental illness. Most of us trust psychiatry to remain immune to fads. And it does, doesn’t it?</br></br>One of the consistently fascinating and disturbing aspects of “Mad, Bad and Sad: Women and the Mind Doctors" is Lisa Appignanesi’s assiduous tracking of the modishness of what might be mistaken for a sui generis discipline. Of course, as anyone who has visited a psychiatric hospital — or ridden the subway — can attest, crazy is what we call people who refuse to conform to accepted norms of behavior. And the definition of nonconformity must change in step with styles of conforming.</br></br>"Mad, Bad and Sad” is, Appignanesi tells her readers, not only “the story of madness, badness and sadness and the ways in which we have understood them over the last 200 years,” but also a survey or tiie mad, bad and sad themselves, the particular women, including Zelda Fitzgerald, Lucia Joyce, Virginia Woolf and many less famous patients, who suffered "frenzies, possessions, mania, melancholy, nerves, delusions, aberrant acts, dramatic tics, passionate loves and hates, sex, visual and auditory hallucinations, fears, phobias, fantasies, disturbances of sleep, dissociations, communion with spirits and imaginary friends, addictions, self-harm, self-starvation, depression" and so on. Phew. A list like this makes a girl grateful that Freud even bothered to risk what such desperate, deluded creatures might want. No wonder the 19th century couldn’t build enough asylums to house them.</br></br>Kathryn Harrison’s "While They Slept: An Inquiry Ini u the Murder of a Family" will be published in June.

text: STRUGGLING as we are with the housing bust, the credit crunch, shrinking consumption, rising unemployment and fal-| tering business investment, we can be forgiven for thinking that all the big shoes have dropped. There is another one up there, however, and it is about to come down.</br></br>State and city governments have yet to shrink the economy; indeed, they have even managed to prop it up; They have quietly maintained their spending at pre-crisis levels even as they warn of numerous cutbacks forced on them by declining tax revenues. The cutbacks, however, are written into budgets for a fiscal year that begins on July 1, a month,away. In the meantime the states and cities, often drawing on rainy-day savings, have carried their share of the load for the national economy.</br></br>That share is gigantic. At $1.8 trillion annually in a $14 trillion economy, the states and municipalities spend almost twice as much as the federal government, including the cost of the Iraq war. When librarians, lifeguards, teachers, transit workers, road repair crews and health care workers disappear, or airport and school construction is halted, the economy trembles. None of that, or very little, has happened so far, not even in California, despite a significant decline in tax revenue.</br></br>"We are looking at a $4 billion cut to public schools and deep cuts that will result in thousands of Californians losing their health care," said Jean Ross, executive director of the California Budget Project, offering a preview of coming hardships. "But the reality is we have not pulled money off the streets yet.”</br></br>Quite the opposite, the states and municipalities have increased their spending in recent quarters, bolstering the nation’s meager economic growth. Over the past year, they have added $40 billion to their,outlays, even allowing for scattered spending freezes and a few cutbacks in advance of July 1. Total employment has also risen. But when the current fiscal year ends in 30 days (or in the fall for many municipalities), state and city spending will fall, along with employment — slowly at first and then quite noticeably after the next president takes office.

The police department put him on leave, and he has lived on Social Security since Mr. Clark, who uses a wheelchair and can walk with a cane, argued, however, that he could do desk work, and he sought help from Equip for Equality, an advocacy group in Chicago, which sued for Mr Clark's reinstatement in 1997 The United States District Court dismissed his claim once, but it is now scheduled for trial in October There are many throughout the department, Mr. Clark said, adding “I’ve done a few of them before when I was in uniform, administrative stuff, like keeping logs and records There’s no question in my mind that there is a place for me where I can continue to make a valuable contribution ” A spokeswoman for the Chicago police force said Mr. Clark was offered a desk job but “he wanted to remain a sworn police officer,” a title reserved for people who can respond to emergencies and fire then guns from a standing position “This is mostly where the dispute comes from,” she said As for Ms. Triano, she always wanted to be a lawyer, and after graduating Phi Beta Kappa from the University of California at Santa Barbara in 1996, she set out to take the law school admittance exam But a hereditary immune-system disorder makes her highly susceptible to colds and infections and prone to diarrhea and vomiting when under stress Because of that, she had always been given access to a bathroom while taking tests in high school and college The Law School Admission Council, which administers the Law School Admission Test, refused to grant her special privileges, she says, even after she submitted medical records from her immunologists and letters from Santa Barbara . In frustration, Ms Triano, 25, started an Internet support group for people who had had similar problems m taking the law exams, and 50 people joined, she says She also complained to the Justice Department, saying her rights for reasonable accommodation of her condition had been violated As a result of similar complaints, she says, the department sued the Law School Admission Council last year in the Eastern District Court of Pennsylvania m Philadelphia to try to force it to change its policy on accommodating students with disabilities Not surprisingly, the council is “in extreme disagreement on whether or not we’ve violated the A D A.,” said Joan E Van rol, its corporate counsel “We’ve complied with all the requirements” in accommodating the complainants, she said, and “in responding to the thousands of other test takers who have requested accommodations.”</br></br>Meantime, though, the experience so upset Ms. Triano that she abandoned law and enrolled in the Ph D. program in disability studies at the University of Illinois.</br></br>Richard Clark, left, is fighting for a job with the Chicago Police Department. William G. Stothers, above, with Cynthia Jones, of the Center for an Accessible Society, says many employers are simply nervous about hiring disabled people.</br></br>into traditional employment fields like law and are getting turned down,” Ms. Triano said “So they’re going into a field where they can get the accommodation they need, which is in the disabled community I’ve seen this happen time and again ”</br></br>The frustrations that Mr. Clark and Ms Triano have encountered mirror a larger and troubling reality despite federal law to protect them against discrimination in hiring and promotion, and despite efforts by companies to recruit and train them and make job sites more accessible to them, the disabled continue to face a huge struggle for full workplace equality The main reason seems to be that although the law has changed, attitudes have not “Clearly, many employers don’t know how to level the playing field and engage people with disabilities in jobs,” said Dr Susanne Bruyere, director of the program on employment and disability at Cornell “We need to infuse all participants — from upper management to supervisors to workers — with new attitudes toward the one in six Americans with disabilities ”

text: September’s act of terrorism was dreadful enough to throw this nation into turmoil and put the new president’s mettle to the test. He needed to calm nerves and stabilize the stock market in the wake of the crisis. He had to pay immediate attention to revamping the country’s transportation system. And he had to address the problem of foreign-born, politically violent individuals wreaking havoc on American soil.</br></br>“They and those like them should be kept out of this country,” he told the Congress, “and if found here they should be promptly deported to the country whence they came.” He added forcefully. "The American people are slow to wrath, but when their wrath is kindled it bums like a consuming flame.”</br></br>The events of that troubled autumn may sound eerily current, but they took place 100 years ago The 1901 assassination of President William McKinley by Leon Czolgosz had thrust Theodore Roosevelt into the nation’s highest office so unexpectedly that he was somewhere up an Adirondack peak when he received the summons to assume power. But he rose to the test so robustly and charismatically that Edmund Morris’s new, second installment in his Roosevelt biography easily conveys the tenor of this presidency. By dint of its subject’s wildly captivating personality, “Theodore Rex” is able to combine the sweep of history and the complexities of statesmanship with the persuasive sense that you, the reader, are there Readers of “Dutch A Memoir of Ronald Reagan” will gladly notice who is not there: Mr Morris While the author felt the need to insert himself into that book as a befud-dhngly half-imaginary character.</br></br>"Theodore Rex” arrives 21 years after Mr. Morris’s Pulitzer Prizewinning first installment, “The Rise of Theodore Roosevelt.” And it is good reason to hope that the next volume will not be so long m the making. But this new book, which moves from 1901 to Roosevelt’s departure from office in 1909, is unavoidably encumbered by the presidency itself, forcing Mr Moms to incorporate into his narrative the wide array of complex, unrelated matters with which any president — especially one this omnivorous m his interests — must deal So the high drama of Roosevelt's early years, which prompt Mr. Morris to observe Continued on Page 7 that "Horatio Alger could not get away with such a story,” necessarily gives way to matters of state.</br></br>These range from Roosevelt's successful efforts to regulate the nation’s trust-bound railroads to his adroit diplomacy in settling the Russo-Japanese War, an accomplishment that brought him the Nobel Peace Prize. They include the tricky maneuvers that made the Panama Canal possible (instead of a proposed Nicaraguan Canal at nearly triple the length) and the enormously successful effort to create national parks (despite the opposition of forces with slogans like "Not One Cent for Scenery”). And Mr. Morris must address the most egregious aspect of the Roosevelt record, his handling of race relations m America at a time when lynchings were commonplace. Though one of his first and most widely criticized acts as president was inviting Booker T. Washington to dine at the White House, he allowed the undue punishment of black soldiers stationed in Brownsville, Tex., to become the worst mistake of his presidential career. As all of this is being dutifully explicated, the lively voices of Roosevelt and his contemporaries (in a book that devotes more than 200 pages to notes and an index) effectively brighten the atmosphere being conjured It is said of Mark Hanna, Roosevelt’s troublesome political rival, "That smile could grease a wagon ” Mr Morris describes Republicans pleased by the president’s policies as “smiling like Wagnerites after a slow performance of 'Siegfried ’ ’’ The Moroccan bandit Rai-suh, whose kidnapping of a putative American nearly set off an international crisis, is said by his captive to be "every inch a man of daring deeds" About a Republican fundraiser, Mr. Morns writes- “Most of Bliss's visits ended with the scratch of a pen writing many zeros on a slip of paper."

text: ■ With grand strategies and firm con-B victions becoming casualties of the stalled, often rocky stock market, some people on Wall Street are reviving a strategy intended to capitalize on such difficult conditions. The approach, called pair trading. is essentially an exercise m extreme stock-picking that seeks to make an investor indifferent to the which way the overall market goes — or whether it moves at all.</br></br>A pair trade means buying a stock that is thought to be undervalued while selling short an equal dollar amount of a similar or related stock, typically of a competitor, that appears overvalued.</br></br>The short position, which is a wager that the stock price will decline, reduces risk by protecting against a market downturn. Offsetting it with the stock that is owned — the long side of the equation — makes an investor neutral to the market and, depending on the picks, more or less impervious to the vicissitudes of a particular industry What’s left are bets on individual stocks.</br></br>If the stock picks are squarely on the mark, an investor can make money on both the long and short sides, and the direction of the the overall market does not matter.</br></br>“It’s actually an all-weather strategy, but it makes more sense in a sideways market,” said Christopher J. Wolfe, equity strategist for pnvate clients at J. P. Morgan Chase. “It works well with companies with similar products or end markets whose stocks are closely correlated, but where there is a valuation disparity.” “Pair trades also are a way to play volatility,” Mr. Wolfe said. That is because any development that strengthens the competitive position of one of the companies versus the other, like a new product, will have a greater impact on the respective stock prices m a volatile market “The correlations become less stable,” he said.

text: Yesterday the Federal Reserve lowered interest rates for the ninth time this year. The federal funds rate, the key tool of monetary policy, is now 2.5 percent — below the level of inflation. The stock market did respond well to the move.</br></br>Still, it is becoming clear that the nation’s economic woes are not going to be fixed simply by continual rate-cutting. The attacks of Sept. 11 caught the Fed at just the wrong time Under the leadership of Alan Greenspan, it had slashed rates by three and a half percentage points between January and August m an attempt to juice up a sagging economy. The effects of rate cuts take a while to kick m, and the nation should have been starting to feel their influence right now. But the terrorist attacks took a big, one-time bite out of the economy that lower lending rates cannot fully address. Quick but careful action from Congress and the Bush administration is going to have to do the rest.</br></br>Cuts in the short-term federal lending rate can help businesses offer consumers easier credit, but they cannot make businesses invest in growth when sales are down, or make consumers suddenly worried about their jobs and portfolios decide to go shopping. Only intelligently targeted government spending — or, to a lesser extent, broad-based temporary tax cuts — can stimulate purchasing.</br></br>Cutting the federal funds rate also cannot lower long-term interest rates if the markets have no confidence in the stability of the federal budget. text: JUST seven or eight years ago Naples was a sleepy if affluent snowbird resort, with a certain WASP-y charm but not much going on. Now, transformed by the stock market boom, it has found a new life as a second or third home for dot-com millionaires. It oozes big, new money, which has overtaken the WASP-iness. Naples is a place where $5 million won't buy much of a house The choice ones start at $8 million, and in the Strand, a new gated community within an already double-gated community, houses go for $11 to $25 million.</br></br>Naples was in the right place at the right time. It was the last nice relatively undeveloped place in Florida when the boom hit, and Its location, once its drawback (practically the last mainland town on the Gulf Coast, the end of the line) became its salvation Fortunately, it had the wherewithal to fulfill its destiny.</br></br>Naples has always been extraordinarily pretty, with bright green St. Augustine grass, tall hedges, banyan trees and those palms that lean at 45-degree angles. But now it has a new look — money. Only Palm Beach can compare, and Palm Beach seems bulky and dated by comparison. One senses too many ghosts in those old mansions. In Naples everything is lighter, more informal. This is the city that lives the real estate catch phrase “casual elegance.” Even the 25-story high-rises that dot the northern end of the beach are airy and almost graceful.</br></br>You’ve heard of boutique hotels, Naples is a boutique town. The restaurants are boutique, the museum is boutique, and the boutiques are really boutique Naples even has a boutique beach While most Florida public beaches are surrounded by sunbaked parking lots, Naples’s seven-mile strand of white sand is backed by millionaires’ mansions, just yards away through some elegantly arranged sea grape. Believe me, such an arrangement adds greatly to the beachgoing experience Yet surprisingly, Naples — which I have visited more than half a dozen times in the past year — can be enjoyed at all price levels. There are brand-new motels out by the Interstate (all the national chains) that are cheap in winter and dirt cheap in summer. There are a number of accommodations downtown that are reasonable and so well placed that you can walk anywhere you need to go — a rarity in Florida and an important consideration for nondrivers, particularly those with comfortable shoes and wide-brimmed hats.</br></br>But a penny pincher loading up on sandwich meat at the 7-EIeven — and yes, there is one, right in the fanciest shopping district in town — would be a little out of sync with the Naples mindset. text: BNFLATION is the bugaboo of bond investors. Each time it climbs, it chips away at the purchasing power of a bond's fixed payout. So it is not surprising that investors have been scooping up Treasury inflation-protected securities, or TIPS, as if they were going out of style.</br></br>But TIPS may be a victim of their own success. As their popularity has grown, their prices have soared — to the point that ordinary Treasury bonds may be a better alternative, some analysts say. “TIPS are a worthwhile addition to a portfolio at a certain price," said James Grant, editor of Grant’s Interest Rate Observer, a newsletter that covers bonds. “At the current price, TIPS offer a meager real return.”</br></br>The bonds’ appeal resides in one significant feature. Unlike regular bonds, TIPS have interest rates with two effective components: one fixed, the other tied to inflation, as measured twice a year by the Consumer Price Index. If inflation rises — as it did in March, with an unexpectedly big price jump of 0.5 percent — so, eventually, does the bond’s yield and principal. But if inflation declines, then the yield and principal value of the bond also falls, though an investor will recoup no less than the par principal amount at maturity.</br></br>TIPS trade like other Treasury bonds, typically in blocks of $1,000. In addition, the Treasury issues I-bonds — savings bonds that come with a fixed interest rate plus a variable, inflation-adjusted component. Like TIPS, I-bonds can be bought directly from the Treasury’s Web site, www.publicdebt.treas.gov, in denominations as small as $25.</br></br>Since TIPS were introduced in 1997, they have provided strong returns. For the last three years, a typical TIPS mutual fund has increased 9.5 percent a year, on average, according to Lipper Inc., which tracks mutual funds.

text: FOR most politicians — Democratic or Republican — the issue of outsourcing jobs to faraway countries is a no-brainer: It’s bad for the United States economy and it’s even worse for their careers, especially in an election year when the work force has just lost more than two million jobs. Outsourcing will ultimately enhance their productivity.</br></br>Yet while debate is raging over globalization’s costs and benefits, Mr. Mankiw’s comments are based on solid, age-old economic arguments. "If other countries can do something cheaper we ought to let them do It, and concentrate on what we can do best."</br></br>Indeed, despite the hemorrhage of jobs since Mr. Bush took office, the past performance of the American economy — particularly the pattern of job creation and destruction over the past several years — supports Mr. Mankiw’s case.</br></br>In many ways, the economists’ argument for outsourcing is as straightforward as the case for importing products. If an Indian software programmer is paid a tenth of an American's salary, a company that develops software in India will save money and — provided competitors do the same — the price of its software will fall, productivity will rise, the technology will spread, and new jobs will be created to adapt and improve it

text: The Labor Department reported on Friday that the economy lost 345,000 jobs last month — an improvement over the much larger monthly losses recorded since October, but still abysmal. In the first year of the recession, from December 2007 to December 2008, wage growth held up relatively well, outpacing inflation. But In May, the growth in weekly paychecks, which captures cutbacks in hours, contracted at a 2.3 percent annualized rate. A combination of rising unemployment and collapsing wage growth can only constrain consum-</br></br>Beyond a generalized sense that “this too shall pass," no one seems to know just how robust employment — good jobs with good pay — will resume. text: In its first annual report, made public in December, 1946, the President’s Council of Economic Advisers declared that the philosophy of the Employment Act of 1946, under which it was created, steered a course between “Spartan fatalism” and the Roman concept of “bread and circuses.” The Council itself, it may be said, has to date endeavored with more than fair success /to adhere to the same general philosophy. The third annual report, which has just made its appearance, is no exception.</br></br>The 1946 report of the Council was devoted chiefly to a discussion of the social-economic theory of sustained employment. A year ago it dealt with the idea of maximum production and the means of achieving it. The present report is primarily an effort to develop a clearer understanding of the Board’s role and the environment within which it functions. “The Council,” it points out, “was not furnished with a clean page upon which to write policies consistent with free competitive enterprise which might contribute to economic stability.” And it adds:</br></br>We could no more neglect programs which have become a settled part of national policy than fail to consider the limits of human and material resources. A great nation has many objectives, and social | and political programs to which the popular voice has assigned supreme importance cannot be set aside in order to simplify the making of purely economic policies.</br></br>The Council cites several examples of this necessity for reconciling economics with broad social policies. Although a free price system is desirable, it points out, it would be unrealistic to proceed on the assumption that farm price supports would be abandoned as a matter of national policy. Again, it notes, the Government’s housing program, with its deliberate promotion of easy credit, is an anomaly at a time when the country is faced with the threat of inflation, but it must be accepted because of the seriousness of the housing shortage. The Government’s bond-support program similarly illustrates the difficulty of stabilizing the economy. “We cannot,” the Council observes on this point, “propose that the inflationary threat be met by action which would create even greater danger.”</br></br>Some may see a touch of “fatalism” in the almost off-hand way in which the Council accepts some, at least, of j these policies as permanent fixtures of American life. This is particularly true in the case of farm price supports. Few persons now, if any, would urge a return to the days of the cynical slogan, “The best cure for 5-cent cotton is 5-cent cotton.” On the other hand, in our farm policy we have long since left the reasonable objective of orderly marketing far behind us. Farm loans, introduced originally so that the farmer would not be compelled to dump" his produce on the market for whatever price it would bring, have now been made so attractive that we are currently witnessing the spectacle of farmers growing crops not for the market but for the loans they will bring.

text: ANN ARBOR, Mich. — Once again, the Burger Court has confounded its critics. The most recent batch of cases, the last to be decided during the tenure of the retiring Chief Justice, defies ideological classification. On issues ranging from capital punishment to sodomy, press reporting of judicial proceedings to tasteless speech at high school assemblies, racial preferences in employment to the separation of Government powers in the task of budget control, the Court has produced a mosaic of decisions that no one could have predicted. The political right is frustrated that a Court appointed almost entirely by Republican Presidents (it has been 19 years since a Democrat named a Justice) should take a measured, complex view of such constitutional issues as religion in the public schools, abortion, affirmative action and capital punishment.</br></br>titled to appoint judges throughout the Federal judiciary whose decisions on these and other issues are predictably in consonance with conservative political ideology.</br></br>The unpredictability of the Burger Court is, in my view, one of its greatest strengths. The constitutional tradition of the United States, a tradition virtually all political factions have a stake in preserving, was built by judges whose decisions disappointed the Presidents who appointed them. Had such Justices as John Marshall, Oliver Wendell Holmes and Charles Evans Hughes been more predictable in the way they decided cases, our constitutional law would be very different than it is, and much the poorer.</br></br>Of course, not all forms of unpredictability contribute to the development of a vital constitutional tradition. text: By ARTHUR KROCK WASHINGTON, March 21 — Whatever may be the facts, as contrasted with the statistics, about the inflationary effect of the steady rise in employment costs, a steady rise in the living costs of the consumer has been a faithful attendant circumstance.</br></br>It is argued by some economists, on the basis of Government statistics, that employment-cost rises in big unionized industries, except when productivity has failed to keep pace, have not been a principal cause of the inflation that now so plainly afflicts the average American family and small business man. But the economists who dispute this analysis make more sense to the average American family that has been asking “how come?” of its purveyors of goods and services and getting the invariable reply that the labor costs of production have "gone up.”</br></br>In the midst of the dust raised by the scuffling economists the only thing in plain sight is the inflation itself. Among the ideas advanced ! to check its minatory growth one has constantly recurred. This is, some large producer of goods should announce that 'for a period—usually one year is proposed—he will not increase the price of his products. The theory is that public opinion will effect emulation by Government, industry and labor, and a “climate” of voluntary controls will be created in which inflation will wither away.</br></br>The President once heard a long discussion of this idea, and, since he abhors Government economic controls, he listened with sympathetic interest. On that occasion the producer suggested as pioneer of the experiment was the United States Steel Corporation. Now it develops that one year after this discussion (it was 1947 and the President was Chief of Staff of the Army) the big steel corporation did make the experiment, in the expanded form of price cutting, and discovered labor would not go along and other units of management yielded to. its pressure for higher and higher wages.</br></br>This history of the failure of an idea was related in a speech made to a national newspaper group in Chicago by Roger M. Blough, chairman of the board of U. S. Steel. Some extracts follow:

And, though he equated the concept of statutory F. E. P. C. with the President’s 1959 request that Congress give a statutory authority to the existing President’s Committee on Fair Employment Practices, the difference between the two is fundamental in fact and in political philosophy.</br></br>That difference is this: the existing executive committee has noncompulsory jurisdiction, and only over complaints of discrimination in the hiring, of labor by holders of contracts for Government projects. But the Federal F.E.P.C, pledged in the Democratic platform would have statutory and compulsive authority, and this would he extended to the hiring of labor in private business. If this type of F. E. P. C. should be legislated, private employers engaged ip business for profit, whose employes number-fifty or more and whose product enters interstate commerce, would be summoned before the commission to defend themselves from any complaint by an (applicant that he had been denied employment because of his national origin, membership in a certain race ! or religious body, etc.</br></br>The master legislative draft in this field was approved by both House and Senate committees in 1950. text: It happens every winter in the housing industry: Plants become idle and employment declines. This seasonal nature of the construction business and in particular the residential market, which peaks in the spring and summer, results in higher costs for the builder, the consumer and the public.</br></br>Residential construction is about twice as seasonal as nonresidential construction. Single-family housing starts are about 50 percent more seasonal than multifamily starts and the Northern sections of the country are about twice as seasonal as the West and the South.</br></br>Blame it on the immutable forces of weather that require removal of snow and ice and special protection and heating for materials and workers, whose productivity is usually somewhat numbed. That has been the conventional wisdom.</br></br>However, a new study, “Seasonal Cycles in the Housing Market: Patterns, Costs and Policies,” by Kenneth T. Rosen, challenges the assumption that the weather is primarily at fault and argues that consumer demand, and builder response and habit, is more responsible. Mr. Rosen maintains that the housing industry could accommodate a more efficient timetable.</br></br>The demand for housing, Mr. Rosen declared, is highly seasonal. Traditional patterns of household formations and moves are remarkably constant, he said. Primary and secondary school-year calendars are major inhibitors of consumer demand for housing as many people wait for the end of a term before getting married and many others are hesitant to move their families during the school year.

text: WASHINGTON — The National Archives, staid repository of the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution and perhaps three billion other historical items, finds Itself at the center of several very current controversies. First there are the Nixon tapes, the disputes . over which seem destined to provide lifetime employment for a quarrel of lawyers. The latest development is a suit to compel the Archives to keep them secret. Then there are the Martin Luther King Jr. tapes. Senator Jesse Helms, Republican of North Carolina, tried to gain access to them in his unsuccessful attempt to raise doubts about the late civil rights leader and thereby block a national holiday memorializing him.</br></br>Finally, there is an argument over the structure of the National Archives itself as its approaches its 50th anniversary next year. Many historians maintain that it should revert to independent status and not continue as a division of the General Services Administration, which operates most Federal buildings. Charges that past G.S.A. administrators — among them Arthur Sampson, an appointee of President Nixon’s — interfered -with the Archives' independence have been behind the debate.</br></br>Shortly before resigning, Mr. Nixon reached an agreement with Mr. Sampson that his tapes would be left in the custody of the National Archives but that Mr. Nixon could determine which tapes might be destroyed, according to Congressional testimony. The agreement was reached without the knowledge of James B. Rhoads, who was then the chief of the archives. Congress intervened and abrogated the agreement, an action that was upheld by the Supreme Court, and the Nixon tapes have remained in the custody of the Archives.</br></br>Some of the tapes, in fact, have become national curios. Each day people go to the Archives and are given headphones with which they may hear Mr. Nixon saying to aides, "It is not easy, but it can be done," when asked whether money could be raised for the burglars who broke into the Democratic headquarters in the Watergate, the burglary that had set into motion the events that led to Mr. Nixon's resignation.</br></br>Congress mandated that the tapes and large numbers of related documents be kept in the Washington area. They are not in the Archives’ huge Romanesque building just off the Mall but rather across the Potomac River in Alexandria, Va., and it is there that 29 former Nixon Administration officials would like them to stay. The Nixon 29, as they are called by Archives employees, include Mr. Nixon’s press secretary, Ronald L. Ziegler; a speechwriter, Patrick Buchanan, and his budget director, Roy L. Ash. They maintain that their rights to privacy would be violated by release of the material, which Congress wanted done as soon as it was catalogued, and assert executive privilege as well. text: Each month the latest figure on the United States index of leading economic indicators is headline news. Usually described as the Government’s foreshadowing statistic because of its tendency to anticipate changes in economic trends a few months ahead of such measures of performance as the gross national product, industrial production or employment, the index achieved great prominence during the recent election campaign. It declined in . August and September after rising for 17 straight months. Thus it dramatized the recent slowdown in economic growth.</br></br>This index, or one very much like it, has been published by the Commerce Department since November 1968. But summary indexes of leading economic indicators have been in existence since 1949. They, have had a long history. Their record of performance and the rationale underlying it have been carefully examined by many, scholars and tested against subsequent experience— a .test that many forecasting schemes have failed to survive.</br></br>By-the same token, it . took a long time for leading economic indexes to . reach the front pages of The New York Times or the television news programs. The development of a new economic statistic often precedes by many years its acceptance and wide use. Public interest also fluctuates. There’s more interest in the leading index when questions arise about the onset or end of a slowdown or recession than at other times. But unless the work of maintaining, testing, and improving such 'data is carried oh continuously, they will not be available when most needed. Moreover, unless' the development work is done long in advance'of the event, the performance record that is essential to proper interpretation of the data will not be available either. This is one case where everyone can agree on the need for planning ahead. "</br></br>Although the development of leading 'indicators in the United States has been proceeding vigorously, the same cannot he said for their development along international lines. Yet the need is apparent. In 1974 (when recession was encompassing a large number of countries) and later (when a widespread recovery was observed) much attention was given, to these developments. The deterioration in the American trade balance this year has been attributed to the earlier and faster recovery here than abroad—Which'raised our imports faster than our exports. Before that, the unusual synchronism among coun-.tries in the boom conditions that characterized 1972 and 1973 was one of the factors on which the double-digit inflation of 1973 and.l974-was blamed.</br></br>But in all this discussion of the international business cycle, which occupied many pages in the press, virtually no attention was paid to leading economic indicators in other countries. One senses that for her, worldly failure is less of a soul-killer than failure to find grace, whenever and wherever it might occur. text: NEARLY three years into the worst employment slump since World War II, many unemployed professionals are finding that the job networks they have been tapping are no longer producing.</br></br>This turn of events — which some call network burnout or network fatigue — appears to be a natural consequence of too many job seekers asking for too many favors. And many people in a position to hire are getting tired of it.</br></br>“It’s a lot like spam," said Diane DiResta, president of DiResta Communications, which assists in career development. "People keep hitting up the same contacts over and over again. But people have a lot more to do these days and are less benevolent than they were in the past. There’s no time for all the requests.”</br></br>Networking has been a highly effective way for many professionals to land a job, and that makes desperate job seekers that much more determined to hit up any and all contacts. According to a recent survey conducted by Bernard Haldane, the national career management firm, 61 percent of responders found their last job through networking while only 3 percent landed a job through the Internet and 16 percent by newspaper listings. text: THE Equal Employment Opportunity Commission handles about 80,000 discrimination claims, called “charges,” each year, though many other acts of discrimination go unreported, experts say, partly because workers think they cannot afford a lawyer or may get fired.</br></br>But workers do not need a lawyer to pursue a discrimination claim, which is free, and some lawyers work on a contingency basis. Laws also protect employees from retaliation by their employer.</br></br>Nonetheless, workers who file a claim will confront many rules and choices in a process that can take many months, If not years, to resolve, and they might have a hard time proving discrimination.</br></br>The E.E.O.C. enforces federal discrimination laws that prohibit sexual harassment; protect equal pay based on sex; prohibit discrimination based on age (40 and older), color, disability, national origin, pregnancy, race, religion or sex; and protect workers from retaliation. Most state and local laws match federal laws and go further. In New York, it's illegal to discriminate based on sexual orientation or marital status.</br></br>As soon as discrimination begins, a worker should record discriminatory words and behaviors, and any witnesses.
